[00:16:37.15] - Taylor

And the photographer was claiming it was his camera, therefore it was his photo. And they said, "no, but you didn't take the photo, the animal did." And because the animal isn't an intelligent creature, it didn't count, and therefore it was a public domain photo. And they're sort of applying the same sort of thinking to AI, which is very interesting because it just— if that's the case, it means that no AI is actually owned by anyone.

[00:01:39.08] - Taylor
But surely all of the data it's trained on is copyrighted, and so therefore—

[00:01:44.12] - Gordon

So if, for example, you take— if you make a song, for example, you can't claim ownership of it as far as copyright goes, but you can, depending on your terms and conditions, have creative and commercial use of it, which is really interesting. If you take a song that AI has written and then re-record it yourself, you're using it as inspiration, and therefore what you create, because you created it, is then your own copyright. I'll go first this week.

So the idea being is I can do a search for whatever I want and it will return results. So if I wanted to say, "what was that hospital appointment that I had last year with my surgeon?" for example. And because it has all the data and it has all the information, I can then you know, it can find it because it's archived and it's scanned the document, things like that. And I got the ScanSnap, from Facebook a while ago, and I've only just managed to now set it up and configure it. But what's been interesting was I took it a step further and I created a tool, a CLI tool, that allowed me to basically interact with Evernote and also with AI through the terminal.

[00:04:02.27] - Taylor
But also I created an MCP server, which is something I hadn't done before, which allowed me to then talk to, you know, using any sort of like AI kind of web app or whatever, like Claude Desktop or ChatGPT, and it has context and tools that it can use to fetch notes, edit tags, create new notes, and also do search and finding for notes. So taking that a step further, rather than just archiving, I can then use it to actually get the data back with my own tools. So Evernote have their own inbuilt search, which is fine, and it actually probably does a very, very good job.. But for me, being able to talk to, you know, have a chat and have it be able to fetch it, you know, in real time and go off and do its own calls has been really helpful, and will be really helpful when I'm just, yeah, trying to find out when something was or what I was doing, etc.

[00:05:00.14] - Gordon
And you've created this tool that will look at the document and give it a bit of context as well, so it'll basically type a note in with a bit of information about what the document is, based on what's in the content, right?

[00:05:16.13] - Taylor
Yeah. So a lot of people will just scan the document. It automatically will OCR it when you scan it in through the scanner. But some things that it doesn't do is add kind of actual written notes that are kind of summarising what the document shows or adding a meaningful title. Instead of just having the file name, it actually has a meaningful title. So when you are searching, you're giving that tiny bit more context, and you can pull out the key things from a document. So if you've got a 20-page document about your mortgage, for example, well, you may want to pull out the highlights of what the rate is and how long it lasts and things like that. So obviously, the context, you can already find it inside of the document. But you're pulling out key things that you may want to reference and be able to find and see at a glance. Alongside that, you know, you can obviously still go through the document and read it yourself, or, you know, it can find it from the document, but it just, kind of neatens it up and, kind of just standardises it.

[00:06:23.25] - Taylor
I wanted to be able to do this but not have just a big dump of just documents. Or if I wanted to create a note, I wanted them to be kind of in a similar format, you know, being labelled the same, being named the same, having a tag system that it follows. So being able to tag everything that's related to the flat inside of one tag. And again, I could just say find me all documents that reference my flat name, for example, and that would work. But going the extra mile to tag it— and again, this is it doing its own tagging through the AI - I can then click on a tag and it'll show me all the documents. It makes it slightly quicker for querying for certain things, whether it's a letter type or if it's a, you know, an online document, if it's a whatever it is, you know, all different types of files you can have essentially.

[00:07:21.20] - Gordon
Well, the paid version of Evernote does have AI search facilities and it's not too bad actually. It's— you can do similar things to what you're saying, but if you've done it all at the time of capture, that's just adding more data, isn't it, that it can then search through?

[00:07:42.14] - Taylor
And you can scan basically as many documents as you want and then say, "categorise everything," and it will go through each file individually, look at the content, kind of get context, and you can give it your own prompt and your own context as well to say like, you know, "I live by myself in a flat, this is the name for my flat, I play a lot of sport," things like that. So it's going to have context about who you are as well. So when it's writing tags, when it's writing the notes, it's got context about you as well without having to go through every single note and get the context.

[00:08:14.02] - Gordon
That's very good. And we should say the ScanSnap is a hardware scanner that allows you to put a bunch of documents into the feeder, press scan and it scans double-sided, so it scans both sides in one pass and then creates, in our case, PDF files and uploads to Evernote. And that's what ScanSnap is. And it's a really good system. I discovered it a long time ago and I've had, I think, 3 ScanSnaps now. Not because there was anything wrong with them. It's just I've upgraded to the latest and the best to make it faster and higher quality and so on. But it's really good and it works very well with Evernote. [00:09:17.12] - Taylor
I don't think so.

[00:09:19.02] - Gordon

So it's, you know, by the time we finished at midnight, it's sort of half a day's worth, you know, maybe even nearly a full day's work, isn't it? It's like 7 hours, isn't it? And so that happens every May, and I go along to it for several reasons. One is that we have lecturers, and it's always good to see lectures on the topic that is something I do as a job. So you can learn from other people, you can listen to what they have to say, you can make decisions as to whether it's something that would work for you or not. And you're getting someone else's experiences, which is a little bit similar to my podcast, FACE: The Podcast, which is a different podcast, and that's designed for family and children's entertainers, and that's a similar sort of thing.

[00:10:50.26] - Gordon
We talk to other entertainers and you can sort of listen to their experiences and take from it whatever you can. But we also have magic shops that go along, so you can sort of have a look and see what they're offering and again decide if there's something you need or want for your show, or something that we end up just putting in our cupboard, which is the other thing magicians are wont to do. They quite often buy things and it goes in a cupboard, never to be seen again. And these things aren't cheap either. Normally they're very expensive. So it's a, you know, it's the longer you do magic, the less you do an impulse purchase. You think about it a bit more and then you make a decision. And sometimes that means you miss out because they've run out, but you do carefully consider things before you purchase them. Just because you don't want to put it in your cupboard and have it never see the light of day again. So we did that. But the thing I think that is the biggest draw for me to these sort of events is meeting all the people.

[00:12:06.00] - Gordon
People that I know, people that I don't know, people that I have already become friends with, people that I make friends with, and some people I just don't have time to speak to, and, you know, next time we have this sort of event, we'll speak to them then and, you know, have a, make a new friend. Mainly because they don't have a two-hour party format in their country. That's not how their birthday parties work. So it's really interesting to listen to different cultures and how they run a party.

[00:13:23.24] - Gordon
And so that was all very exciting. And we had a cabaret act. We had a guy called Spencer Jones who plays the part of Kemp in Upstart Crow, which is a TV comedy by Ben Elton, which funnily enough, I'm watching at the moment. [00:14:10.14] - Taylor
Nice.

[00:14:11.13] - Gordon
So that's Trix. Used to be called Trix in the Stix. Now it's just called Trix because it's in a city centre. [00:00:09.11] - Gordon
Hello.

[00:00:09.20] - Taylor
Hello.

[00:00:10.05] - Gordon
My name is Gordon from Drayson Design.

[00:00:11.29] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

[00:00:14.00] - Gordon
And welcome to "This Week with Taylor and Gordon," a weekly podcast and vidcast where we talk about things that have affected our businesses over the last seven days. And thank you so much for joining us. And welcome to all those new people that we got from our trip last week, which we shall come to in just a moment. How's your week been?

[00:00:33.12] - Taylor
It's been very good.

[00:00:34.12] - Gordon
Yeah, it's been a busy week. We say that all the time. And we tried to do an episode, but, well we thought we might try and do an episode, but we were both very busy and just didn't manage to do it last week. You know, we had all these good intentions. We always do, don't we?

[00:00:53.07] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:00:54.02] - Gordon
And then we just get really busy and, you know, we're just not able to do an episode. So here we are back again after two weeks. And let's get straight into our topics. Would you like to go first or shall I?

[00:01:05.08] - Taylor
You can go first this week.

[00:01:06.26] - Gordon
So this week I'm going to talk about Pop! The Bubble Convention. Now, this is where Taylor and I were last week. We were basically filming the whole of the conference or the convention, which we got there on Tuesday evening last week. We were there filming on Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, and then the show on Saturday evening. So it was a huge event. The talks that were going on on the Wednesday, Thursday and Friday were in up to four rooms at a time. And we had to film all sessions which were 45 minutes long with sort of 15 minutes break between them, and then a lunch break of about an hour. I didn't get a lunch break many days. Did you?

[00:01:57.14] - Taylor
I tried to take a break.

[00:01:59.10] - Gordon
Okay, well, that's good. So Taylor took two rooms, I took two rooms. And I mainly only had one room to deal with because the other room was either a room that was extended to the room I was in, so it was a bigger room if there were more people needed, if we needed the space for more people, or it was a bubble lounge, and that was just sort of a place to hang out and do bubbles with your friends. So I only really had one room, which is just as well because we were taking all the footage and all the recordings that were internal on all the microphones that we gave the speakers and putting them into the computer. And the aim was to try and do it between the sessions so that it gave me the opportunity to then edit those during the next session. That sort of didn't really work very well on the first day because we were using DJI Mic 3s and there's no connection. We couldn't figure out how to get the audio off them. So they have internal recording and we just couldn't figure out how to get the recordings off.

[00:03:11.21] - Gordon
Turns out you put them both into the charging box, leave the lid open, plug in a USB C and they show up as drives on your computer, which is great. And we figured that out first thing on the, on the second day that we were there. So I managed to get all the audio from the previous day off so I could then edit all of the rooms three and four, which Taylor was doing and in charge of. We had three cameras. I had my DSLR in my room that was recording onto my Ninja Blade and that has been upgraded so we now have an SSD in there, 2 terabyte SSD and that worked really well. We had some corruption when we were filming the pantomime and I don't know quite what the problem was with that, but I had absolutely no corruption at all. Everything that I've done and I haven't quite finished, but everything I've done came out wonderfully and beautifully without any corruption. So I was very pleased with that. You had an iPhone 16 Pro that you were using in one of the rooms and then in the last room, because we only had three sessions at any one time going on, even though there were four rooms, which is just as well because, you know, that was busy enough.

[00:04:28.25] - Gordon
But the last room had the DJI Osmo Pocket 3 running. Now each of these devices were capturing ambient sound and the microphones that we had on each speaker was capturing the sound for them. So when I was synchronising them all together with Final Cut and making multicam clips, it was taking the audio from the microphones, it was taking the audio from the cameras, syncing them all together, and I was basically just lowering down as far as I could the ambient sound, unless I needed the ambient sound for example, when people were asking questions, and keeping the audio from the microphone from the speaker nice and high. In fact, I boosted it and that came out really, really well. You could hear the speakers nice and clearly. You could hear background noise of people in the audience, so you knew they were there, but it meant that the speaker's voice was coming through nice and clear, which was the most important thing. Now, after the three days, I managed to get two of the days worth of videos edited and uploaded. They had a reasonably fast internet speed, so that was good. I can't remember what the speed was. Do you remember testing?

[00:05:47.28] - Taylor
I think we got about 80.

[00:05:49.12] - Gordon
80 up.

[00:05:50.14] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:05:51.20] - Gordon
Okay, 80 upload. So that wasn't too bad. They were going up quite quickly, and they were about 4 to 500 megabytes per file once I'd compressed them. So it didn't take too long for them to upload. And then I started on the next one, and I got the first two days worth done, which was about 27 videos. And the last day only had four sessions. Then the Saturday we had, my 360 camera, which creates huge files. That was out in the park where they were bubbling in the park. And then the evening show I've yet to do as well. And that is two cameras. And I used my tape camera for one of those and the Ninja Blade with the DSLR for the other camera. So those need capturing and also editing, and synchronising. So still a little bit of work to do, but, boy, was it hard. Not hard work. It was. It was hard work. It was long days, but yeah, it sort of took all the equipment we needed. Eventually. Yeah, there was a couple of things that I didn't have that other people did have, so that was really good. We managed to fix that. There was a keyboard issue and there was a mouse issue, but we managed to figure that out. In fact, I think I borrowed yours, didn't I?

[00:07:16.12] - Taylor
Yeah. And then you found yours.

[00:07:17.22] - Gordon
And then I found mine. Yeah.

[00:07:19.10] - Taylor
At the end of the convention.

[00:07:20.17] - Gordon
Yeah, I know. Just as we were packing, I found my mouse, which is so funny, but I'm glad I found it because that's one less thing I've now got to buy and replace. My keyboard is a wired keyboard, and I removed it from the computer room into the kitchen so I could test it all and make sure that I had all the cables and everything was working and my keyboard just wouldn't work. It made no sense. I ended up having to get a very old keyboard. And that did work. And I took that with me, but it wasn't ideal because it's, you know, it's a lot more clunky when you type on the keys. And I wanted the really nice keyboards that they use because it's a lot easier. And you had one which was wireless and that worked. So we managed to do that, which was great. So, yeah, I'm hoping to try and get most of the footage edited so that we can upload that next week and then that's that project finished. But yeah, so far so good. Any comments about the event? Because you were there helping which was really lucky.

[00:08:28.23] - Taylor
It wasn't something that I was kind of interested in, as in that wasn't the reason why I went, but I did find it interesting.

[00:08:36.20] - Gordon
And you still managed to get sort of your normal week's work done effectively because you were only having to start and stop cameras and then move them in. So it was like a little break from your work. But the rest of the time you could just come and help, couldn't you?

[00:08:52.08] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:08:52.26] - Gordon
Sorry. The rest of the time you could just do your own work. So we didn't really take away too much of the time that you needed to work on your projects. So that was really good. And we made some new friends, didn't we?

[00:09:05.01] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:09:05.22] - Gordon
Some of them will have started following us now on our YouTube channel for This Week With. So welcome. I know Harvey, who was a great help actually. Harvey was doing other video. He was doing like a more documentary style and he was just wonderful. He helped move cables and power supplies and, you know, offered all of his equipment all the time. Whenever we, you know, were looking to think, try and figure out how we were going to do things, he supplied us with drinks, which was lovely, all out of his own pocket.

[00:09:42.21] - Gordon
And so if you are watching this, Harvey, thank you very much. We are really grateful to all the help you gave us while you were there. You were just wonderful. And you know, we've got a story about Wetherspoons. If you see either of us ask us about that, we'll tell you about it. Way too long to go on the podcast. So that was my week. Tell me, what are you, like, what would you like to talk about?

[00:10:06.14] - Taylor
So this week I have been upgrading a couple of things for my smart home.

[00:10:11.27] - Gordon
Okay, that's good.

[00:10:13.08] - Taylor
So first of all, we went to Ikea on Sunday and they have brought out some new buttons and other smart things. So I went and bought a couple of them to give them a try and see how they worked. But I also had a couple of use cases for them where putting them in places that are useful but also being able to use them to trigger routines and things like starting my day, for example, having them automatically open all the curtains or turning on all the lights, you know, starting, unlocking the front door or whatever it is so that my, you know, flat is ready to go for the morning. And then I also bought a relay. So it's a smart relay. And what it does is it goes in the back of a light switch and it allows you to make your dumb light switch into a smart switch. A lot of people would kind of say, "why do you need that? You can control it from your phone." But a lot of people that come around don't know you have smart tech in your house. And so they will be looking to use the light switch.

[00:11:25.26] - Taylor
And what happens is they press the light switch and it doesn't do anything, so they press it again and they end up turning and cutting the entire power to the light switch. And why that is an issue is because if you have automations and routines set up, if your power has been cut to the light switches or the light bulbs, none of your automations are going to work. So what I wanted to do was to be able to add the functionality of a normal light switch that people are used to, but make sure that it's not going to break any of my automations, break any of the routines that are set up to work in the flat. And the other one is that the bathroom doesn't have, or I can't put a smart bulb in the bathroom because it has a kind of proprietary custom fitting with LEDs and things like that. And so what I can do is I can put a motion sensor in there and I can have it so that it can trigger and simulate somebody pressing the light switch. And this is a way that I can then control the bathroom lights, even though they aren't smart lights, and make them smart.

[00:12:34.05] - Gordon
So when you walk in, the sensor will see you and turn the light on by triggering power to your sensor in the plug and then when you leave doing the opposite.

[00:12:46.24] - Taylor
Exactly. And the bathroom also has a fan which you can actually control and turn on and off, but it's only powered on when the light switch is on. So the fan won't run if the power to the light switch isn't basically on. And so I can put one in there as well so that if I have any humidity, if it goes above a certain threshold, you can have it turn on the fan, but obviously you have to turn on inside of your automation the light to the bathroom, which is fine because you can then just turn it off once it's finished. And you just make sure that when you want to turn the fan on, you have to turn the light switch on as well.

[00:13:24.20] - Gordon
Yeah. And also if you've got, you know, the need to have the fan on for a little bit longer after you leave the bathroom, then you can do so, you know, if you've had a shower, for example, or you know, somebody's, you know, been to the toilet or whatever, and you want to get rid of any odours so you can, you can have it so it turns the lights off effectively, but leaves the fan on?

[00:13:50.28] - Taylor
So the light switch has to be on for the fan to be able to run.

[00:13:53.17] - Gordon
And therefore the light has to be on. Ok.

[00:13:55.04] - Taylor
But it can keep the light on until the fan is finished and then turn the light switch off with the fan.

[00:14:00.18] - Gordon
Yeah, okay, that's very good.

[00:14:03.02] - Taylor
So, yeah, just looking at ways to kind of automate things and make things a bit more user friendly. I also plan to add some light strips above and below the kitchen kind of, or above the kitchen counter. And again, that light switch is actually controlled on the other side of the room, which is a bit of a pain because it's nowhere near where you are. But also if I want to have them come on automatically when I walk in the room at night, for example, it's quite a nice thing to have, but I have to make them smart to be able to do that. Currently they are wired to a broken smashed light that used to kind of work, but doesn't really anymore. So I want to get that replaced and get a electrician in to.

[00:14:51.12] - Gordon
And that's another good use of the switches that you bought from Ikea, right?

[00:14:55.26] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:14:56.07] - Gordon
So these are called Bilresa, I think that's correct. And they do several different types. This is using Matter and connect to Home Assistant. I also got one and I was playing with it during the week. My switch, I've got one in my office now. And the switches, it has two switches, two buttons, I should say, on the switch. So you can single press, double press and hold for three seconds. So each button gives you three different switches you can turn on if you like. So that's six in total. Six actions you can take. And so I've got mine in my office. The top button, single press turns on my lights. So if for whatever reason my automation hasn't seen me and hasn't turned on the light, sometimes if I walk out of the room and then come back in again just as the sensor has triggered, saying, "there's no one here, turn it off." There's that little gap of time where it doesn't then see me and it leaves the lights off. So I can now just press the button and the lights will come on. If I want to turn them off, because maybe I'm wanting to watch something on the screen on or I want to watch something on the tv, the single tap on the second button will turn them off. If I double tap on the top one, it will turn my TV on and the Sky box and change my sound system to use the TV so that it does that automatically all in one go. And then double clicking on the bottom button will. Will reverse that and turn it all off. And then holding on the top button will boost my heating in the office, which is a feature I already have, which basically sets it to 2 degrees higher than it's currently set to. So you can get that boost for half an hour. And then single, sorry, holding on the bottom button or the second button turns all my lights to my watching TV setting, which is blue lights. Now, I don't necessarily want to trigger that when I turn the TV on because I might be doing work and just having the TV on in the background, but if I specifically want to sit and watch something, I can then just press and hold on the second button and all my lights go blue, which is a great colour to use when you're watching tv because it really brings the brightness down, but you still have a bit of brightness in the room. So you're not just staring at a TV screen, which is, you know, not necessary in your case because you've got your ambient lighting.

[00:17:34.27] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:17:35.20] - Gordon
But, yeah, they're really good. I'm going to set one up in the lounge as well so that it will turn the TV on and turn the TV off so that we don't necessarily have to use Alexa. So if, for whatever reason, Alexa is no longer working or, you know, an update has killed it, which we've had in the past, then at least we've got the buttons you can just press. And they're really good because they've got little sticky bits and a sort of metal bit that you can put anywhere. And then these are magnetised and they've got rechargeable batteries in them.

[00:18:06.14] - Taylor
Nice.

[00:18:07.06] - Gordon
So they've got lots of new devices in Ikea. So go and have a look. They've got door and window sensors, they've got water sensors, they've got a Matter hub and I think there's a few other things as well. So go and have a look at those. But, yeah, really good. Well done. Anything else you want to say on that?

[00:18:26.22] - Taylor
I don't think so.

[00:18:27.21] - Gordon
Thank you for joining us. As always, if you're on YouTube, please like, share and subscribe.

[00:18:35.06] - Taylor
You can also go to our website thisweekwith.co.uk to find all of our past episodes.

[00:18:39.26] - Gordon
And if you would prefer to listen to us, we're on all the major podcast platforms and your smart speaker. Just ask them to play "This Week With Taylor and Gordon," and you'll get our latest episode. All being well, we'll be back with you next week at 1pm on Friday. Until then, my name is Gordon and I'm from Drayson Design.

[00:19:00.19] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

[00:19:03.04] - Gordon
Goodbye.

[00:19:03.22] - Taylor
Bye.

And then we're basically there Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, and coming home on the Sunday. And during that time, there are speakers who are going to be speaking on lots of different topics. I'm not sure if it's going to be an extra fee and those who are at the event get them for free, because a lot of the events are happening at the same time.

[00:02:24.25] - Gordon
So similar to Blackpool, in fact, there are two events, and sometimes three events, happening at the same time. And so Taylor and I, between us, have got to make sure we cover all of those events and film them all. Now, this is quite a lot of planning in my case, because I've got to make sure that we've got cameras available for each venue. I've got to make sure we collect good quality sound. And we also, because there's about, I think there's about 30ish sessions that happen over the four days, plus a theatre show, we've got to make sure that we capture everything and then edit it as we go and then upload it, because otherwise I'm going to either run out of storage space on various devices that I'm going to be taking with me, SSDs and so on, or I'm going to just end up with a whole tonne of work to do. And if there's a problem, I need to know about it urgently when we start so that it can be fixed for future sessions. That way we're not going to mess up all the recordings. Because the worst thing you can do is get home from an event and then find that for some reason it wasn't recording.

[00:03:51.20] - Gordon
It's a one-off event. It's not like you can go back and do it again. So it's really important we do it at the time. So the plan is to take along my main desktop computer. And after each session, we will collate. I think there's like 15 minute break between each session. So during that time, we'll collate the footage. Taylor will be in one room, I'll be in another room. And then when there's three sessions, I'm going to ask Taylor to do the third one as well, because I'm going to be taking the footage that we've just had in the last session, which could be two or three events. And then during the session that's going on, I will be bringing all the data in and making sure they're all synchronised with the audio and then exporting them and uploading them, so that by the time we finish the next session, hopefully all of the previous sessions are done and dusted and uploaded. And that way we can make sure that we keep ahead of everything. But there's a lot of tech that I need to take with me because we're going to use the DJI microphones, which we're going to give to each speaker.

[00:05:12.02] - Gordon
Now, I've only got four of those, so we need to plan ahead. And if there's not going to be a microphone for someone during maybe the sessions when there's three going on at once, and maybe there's two or three people in one of them, which is going to cause me problems. I need to then find a way to record another way. Just maybe that because we've run out of microphones, the audio is just going to be ambient audio. We just have to make do with that. [00:06:32.04] - Gordon
And the plan, I think, will be to potentially bring everything or lock everything away or take it back to the room at the end of the day and then bring it back down again in the morning, which is, again, a bit of set up required. But I think it's going to be fun.

[00:06:50.09] - Taylor
Yeah, it should be good.

[00:06:51.05] - Gordon
And I get to spend time with Taylor, which is lovely. Always a good thing to do. And we get to have a bit of fun. We get to go out for meals. We get to watch the show. And again, what we might do is have a couple of angles at the show just so that we've got bases covered, all bases covered. And then the show will be, hopefully, the only thing I have to edit when I get back, because that's going to be the Saturday night, and there will be no time to edit that. Plus, if we're using multiple angles, that's also going to make it difficult. So, yeah, we'll do that when we get back. So, yeah, that's going to be next week. We may or we may not be able to do a This Week With. I mean, it'd be quite fun to do one there because it's going to be a different location and different backdrop, and we might even speak to other people that are there. There's a gentleman called Damian who's organising it, and it might be quite nice to get his thoughts on how it's going and so on. But we'll have to see.

[00:07:50.14] - Gordon
It all depends because obviously, it's all time that we may or may not have. So we'll have to see. The days are quite full. There's a lot of sessions going on, so we need to make sure that that is our focus. So we may be with you, we may not. We'll have to wait and see. Are you looking forward to it?

[00:08:10.08] - Taylor
Yeah, it should be really good.

[00:08:11.16] - Gordon
Yeah, it's going to be a bit of fun. And if Taylor takes his laptop along with him, as long as he's starting and stopping the recordings and then bring them to me, he can also get on with work as well while he's there, which is one of the reasons you're coming, isn't it? Because you're not taking a week off work. You're actually going to be doing things. So that's my topic for today. What would you like to speak about?

[00:08:33.04] - Taylor
So this week I want to talk about a little app I built called CinemaSync. So CinemaSync is a little app that I built to solve a problem that we both faced. So we go to the cinema once a week and we always say to the other person, "What do you fancy seeing this week?" And we essentially just look on the Cineworld website for the day that we're going, have a look, see what films there are and just pick a couple of them and just send them in a text message. We then have to then go to the website, find the film, find the trailer, do a bit of research about the film, who's in it, and things like that. And a bit of a faff.

[00:09:15.14] - Gordon
Yeah.

[00:09:16.01] - Taylor
So I built a little app that allows you to search for any film, and it will essentially put it into a review timeline.

[00:09:27.16] - Gordon
It's a comparison thing, isn't it? Anyone who's been to one of these sites where, like Currys for example, do it because I was on it today. You can choose different products and you can compare them and it just shows them next to each other with the specs. It's a bit like that, isn't it?

[00:09:41.20] - Taylor
Yeah, it shows you the poster, it shows you the title, genres, ratings from IMDb and things like that, who's in it. I built this. [00:02:14.27] - Taylor

And it's the same idea. And I've been setting up my own dashboard to be able to show my upcoming calendar events. So if I've got meetings or if I've got playing tennis or squash, it has the time I need to leave and how long the traffic will take. It has things like my heating, so it shows me all of the heating in the flat, but also it shows me the current temperature and also if it is heating and what the target temperature is; the humidity, so I can monitor that. [00:03:30.28] - Taylor

[00:03:51.20] - Gordon
It's like an up to date whiteboard, really, isn't it? Where you can make notes and things that are important that are coming up, but it's automated. It does it for you and it updates itself. [00:04:15.22] - Taylor
Yeah, so a lot of people have done this and they use a Home Assistant dashboard. The reason I created my own page and a pull in from Home Assistant was because I wanted to be able to add other integrations. So for example, there's a really good app called parcel, which allows you to track the status of all your parcels that you've been delivered, and they actually have an API available. Now, you could integrate this into Home Assistant. You can pretty much integrate most APIs via webhooks and things like that. However, the UI is a bit clunky. You're limited to the widgets and the UIs that they have. Everything has to be put on a grid. [00:05:40.08] - Taylor
There's other services rather than Home Assistant that do these things. And again, they're more geared to people that can't code or don't want to. But for me, I wanted to have full control, be able to integrate with anything I wanted and be able to control what displays - I can have things on the weekend show that don't need to be shown during the week or vice versa. And so for me, being able to have full control was the biggest upside.

[00:06:06.23] - Gordon
That's very good. And have you got a way, I guess not easily, to use a link so that you can go to another page and see other data? Is there a way to set that up? Maybe you can trigger it using your voice or something.

[00:06:25.01] - Taylor
So I could send triggers from other places. Again, it's just sending a web hook. So if you had, because it's a web page, if you had your page listening for a certain endpoint and you then trigger it from anywhere, from your phone, from a button that you then trigger an endpoint to, you could do that. You could have it on a Timer, so you could say every five minutes, change the screen, and you could then have a whole page for your finances. If you've got Stripe payments and you've got a product that you can see real time data, you could see orders come in. There is also, you can use the remote. It is essentially a browser, so you can navigate it and you click on buttons. The experience is limited. Essentially, I have a keyboard with the left and right arrow keys and the enter button. So, I could add buttons that I could press and it would then toggle and I could manually do it. But yeah, there's lots of different ways I could do it if I wanted to.

[00:07:30.07] - Gordon
I mean, that sounds like a really good use case for a touch screen, doesn't it?

[00:07:35.11] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:07:35.26] - Gordon
Being able to have this display and then being able to touch on it to see other things.

[00:07:41.05] - Taylor
I mean, a lot of this was I had a spare TV that I didn't need anymore and I want to make use of it. And I also always wanted to have this dashboard always on available for me. So I just made use of what I've got. And obviously, if you're going to do it from scratch, then yeah, you probably would buy a better TV. I've had to hack my way around to be able to turn the TV on and off with a smart plug because it doesn't detect the firestick turning on and off automatically. But whatever you've got, you make use of it.

[00:08:14.26] - Gordon
Yeah, of course. That's really useful. And I look forward to seeing the progress of it and how it changes over time.

[00:08:22.25] - Taylor
And the nice thing, because it's a website, I can do all the development on my computer and I can actually preview it in my computer before having to push the changes. So once you push the changes, it goes to the live site, but I can see all the changes on my computer.

[00:08:38.17] - Gordon
And I'm guessing you could also view the page on your computer or your phone wherever you happen to be as well, which is quite cool. That's really good. Anything else you want to say on that?

[00:08:49.26] - Taylor
I don't think so. I got the idea from people that have posted on social media. Our friend Marc also had one for his business where he had lots of metrics. His were more business-focused because they were in the office. But I love the idea of them to look up and see things that were updating in real-time and live.

[00:09:09.16] - Gordon
Very good. So my topic today, we're going to talk about Blackpool a little bit more. I went to Blackpool last week on the Wednesday, and the first day of the conference was the Thursday. So it was Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday. So a day longer than it has been in the past. And these days are taken up of getting up for breakfast. I was getting up about 10 past 8-ish, down for breakfast with everyone else. We had a long table for the whole of our group, which was really nice. We could just sit down and have breakfast, discuss what we were going to be doing that day, and then go and get ready to leave. And then we were heading up to the winter gardens, and there were talks, there were lectures, they were not the talks, lectures. They were shows. There were a lot of people selling magic, things that they'd come up with. A lot of people, about 5,000 magicians with multiple things happening at the same time. So you had to pick and choose. I was a VIP. I paid extra to be a VIP, as did all of our group, which meant that we basically got to go into lectures and things 10 minutes before everyone else who wasn't a VIP.

[00:10:33.26] - Gordon
So we were pretty much guaranteed a seat for any lecture we wanted to go to, which it was about £90 more to get that. But the benefit was that we could be sitting down chatting and go, "oh, look at the time we got to go. We got the lecture in 20 minutes." And just be able to walk straight in without queuing and walking past this huge long queue. For some of them, they were really, really big. And then in the evenings, there were shows. There were, again, a selection of shows you could go to. And then the main show in the theatre, which they had two sittings, an early one and a later one. And then back to the hotel to have drinks and getting to bed really late because you're chatting with people, you're talking magic, you're talking about what happened during that day, showing people what you've got, showing things that you've learnt, not getting to bed until about four o'clock in the morning, getting up at eight o'clock in the morning to go for breakfast, and so it continues. So my sleep is very much in debit at the moment, and I'm still recovering even now, even though it was nearly a week ago.

[00:11:47.00] - Gordon
But yeah, your body gets a bit bombarded with weird eating times, lots of alcohol, which I don't normally do, but I was having lots of Bacardi and cokes and Bailey's when I didn't want to have a big drink. So yeah, I had a lovely, lovely time. But the main takeaway for what I want to talk about today is taking action. We've spoken about this before, but you come away from these events with lots of ideas, lots of new things to play with, lots of ways that you can improve your business. And if you just let them sit there and do nothing, then you are wasting an opportunity. You want to start using what you've learnt. You want to start talking to people that you've spoken to, make contact with them. If you've said you're going to send them something or you're going to talk to them about something, do it. Put it in your diary. Make sure... I can never get that word. Diaryise? Put it in your diary.

[00:12:52.16] - Taylor
Diarise.

[00:12:53.11] - Gordon
That's the word. Diarise. A meeting with them. Make sure you get it in the diary. Make sure you follow up. If you have made contacts and networking for a product or a service or something like that, get in contact with them, follow up. It's this time now where you look at it and you go, "Do you know what? I'm really tired. I had pretty much a week off work," except it's not, obviously, because it's part of work, but you've had a week out of the office. And now you feel like, "Do you know what? I just I want to relax and do something different and not think about it." And by the time you come back to thinking about it, several months have passed. And sometimes the iron that was hot is now stone cold, and it's past the point when you need to actually do something. So make sure you come away, make a list of points that you need to look at, things you need to do, and then just work your way through them. Otherwise, as I said, you've got lots of missed opportunities, and sometimes you will have defeated the reason for going.

[00:14:06.02] - Gordon
We have this with WordCamp. It's quite a tiring experience, but it's a lot of fun, and you come away with lots of great ideas. But unless you take action on them, you forget them. You maybe don't do what you need to do to push your business forward or to make your service better or to improve something that you're already doing, a process maybe. So, yeah, it's a really important point. What do you think?

[00:14:37.09] - Taylor
Yeah, I think it's definitely important, and it's also important to make notes at the time. Having to try and hold on to those thoughts and then remember them later when you go, "Oh, what was that great idea I had?" It's also going prepared, making sure you're prepared when you go. [00:15:27.11] - Gordon
Yeah, it's good. It's about having a process again, isn't it? Process for making notes on things to improve. We've got our WordCamp coming up soon. I think it's June. And that is... I've got two... And me as well.

transcript:
[00:00:00.00] - Gordon
Hello.

[00:00:09.15] - Taylor
Hello.

[00:00:10.02] - Gordon
My name's Gordon from Drayson Design.

[00:00:11.29] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

[00:00:13.29] - Gordon
And welcome to "This Week With Taylor and Gordon," a weekly podcast and vidcast where we talk about things that have affected our businesses over the last seven days. And thank you for joining us.

[00:00:23.11] - Taylor
Welcome back.

[00:00:23.28] - Gordon
It's been an interesting week for me. I've had a few bits and pieces going on, things that I've had to finish up, but no big news, really. Any news from your end?

[00:00:38.14] - Taylor
No.

[00:00:39.02] - Gordon
No? Okay, let's get straight into our topics. Would you like to go first or shall I?

[00:00:43.23] - Taylor
I'll go first this week.

[00:00:44.23] - Gordon
Off you go.

[00:00:45.21] - Taylor
So this week I want to talk about essentialism. So I've been reading a book called "Essentialism," and it's about being specific about what you choose to do in both your personal and, I guess, your business or your work life, and not being afraid to say no. I think a lot of people are guilty of or the way that the world has formed is that saying yes to everything is the best thing to do because it opens up the most opportunities, the most things. And we just think, "Yeah, I can do that. I can take it on." If you're working in the corporate world, for example, you just say yes because you want to please people. If you don't do it, no one really does it or it doesn't get done. And the whole point of essentialism is having key values or core values and asking yourself every time you're faced with a decision to say yes or no to anything, really, is "does that get me closer to what I want to do?" Whether that's some principles that you have and you want to live out or whether that's a mission statement that you've set in your company or for yourself.

[00:02:09.29] - Taylor
And making sure that if you do say yes, can you, do you have the bandwidth? Can you actually afford to do it? Not in a monetary sense, but in a time sense. I think that's the biggest thing. Obviously, a lot of people, as you get older, as you get busier, as you earn more money, time is the biggest constraint that we have. And you want to make sure that you're doing stuff that not only excites you and makes you want to get up in the morning to work on it, but also earns you the money. There's a couple of people I know that have taken on projects that don't actually earn them any money or they outsource 80% of the work. And they're not actually making much of a profit, but they're still running around, replying to the emails, they're managing the project, but actually not getting compensated in a way that actually would reflect the amount of time and effort that goes into it, even though they're not ones doing the actual bit of work. And it got me thinking about what do I want to work on? What do I want the legacy?

[00:03:20.25] - Taylor
What are the things that I want my business, or what do I want to focus on? So I've been having a real think and just trying to declutter. I start lots of projects or have done in the past and clearing them out and either saying, "yes, I want to do that. That is a project I want to do." Whether it's personal or a business project or client project. Or "no, it was a nice idea, but actually, it doesn't actually get me any closer to something that I want to be able to do or achieve" and just deleting it, hard cold deleting it. No archiving, no, "I'll come back to that later, I'll leave it lingering in there," just gone. If it's that important, it will get added back or it will find its way back to me in whatever capacity that is. Do you find anything like that, that you...

[00:04:13.19] - Gordon
Um, yeah. I mean, sometimes you say yes to be kind to someone, and maybe they're having a tough time, and maybe you feel sorry for them, and you think, "right, well, I'll try and help them."

[00:04:27.23] - Gordon
And that could be the time that you could spend doing other things that, as you say, might be more profitable or might be more exciting or interesting to you. But then there is also the flip side of that, where you do things because you want to do them, not because they're earning you money. There are several things that I do. For example, I do the posters and the programmes for the pantomime that I do every year. Now, I don't get paid for that. That's something I do because I want to do it because I know if I don't do it, what we have just won't be any good because there's no one else with the skills and the ability to do it. And I really enjoy it. It's something that I quite enjoy doing. It's a nice portfolio piece that I can use if I want to, to show that my design has been used many, many years running for lots of different productions. And I quite enjoy doing that side of it. So, as you say, it's all about whether you want to do it, and that's whether-

[00:05:34.14] - Taylor
Not everything has to be monetary-based. But obviously, if you are doing stuff for people, like you said, you want to help people, but actually it causes more issues because actually you can't do it to the same level that you want to, the same quality, and something has to give. You either give the client a poor experience because you hold the project ongoing for a longer time because actually your standards are a certain length, or you have to compromise on your quality and then give something that the client may be happy with, but you're not happy with. But it doesn't always have to be monetary, could just be something that is close to you, something that you are passionate about. But yes, it's not taking on everything, right?

[00:06:19.29] - Gordon
And as is always the way, there are some exceptions when you get requests from friends or family. You need to be careful that you don't get taken advantage of because that is something that friends and family don't mean to do, but quite often end up doing, if you see what I mean. They ask for something little and that little thing grows into something huge and big and takes up a huge amount of time. But you also want to make sure that you're keeping the family and your friends, family and friends. You're not alienating them by just saying no to everyone all the time. We've just finished a project for a family member, and we didn't really make any money out of it at all, but it was a nice project to do. I think we both learned quite a bit from it, as in not to say no next time. That's not what I mean. What I mean is we learned quite a bit in the way of new technology, new ways of doing things, things that we can take into new projects. Yeah, new tools. We had to buy a new tool for this, which will definitely be used in the future.

[00:07:40.06] - Gordon
So, yeah, it's an interesting concept, but there is that fine line, especially with family and friends, where you just want to tread very carefully and be-

[00:07:49.18] - Taylor
I mean as long as you explain, say, "I would love to help you, but I just don't have the time and I can't give you the attention that you need." I think as long as you explain your reasonings and as long as they're valid and not just "no, because I can't be bothered," then I think people are understanding.

[00:08:05.29] - Gordon
And maybe give them another option. Give them someone else who could help, possibly, because then you're moving a project or a request from you to someone who's not a member of your family or a friend. And therefore, if it's important to them, they might still go ahead with it, but with someone else. And you're not then going to be in the way or do it because it's going to take forever and you're going to do it in your free time, which is never a good thing. If you ever get asked to do something for friends or family and you say, "I'll do it in my free time." Well, that will never happen. I've been there and done that. It just gets pushed out the way and other things get put in front of it. It's not good for either side, basically.

[00:08:50.13] - Taylor
Yeah. So this week was essentially decluttering of things that I've either said yes to and just giving people updates on where things are, or saying no to. And most of these no's have been my own personal projects that I've thought about, gone, "that'd be a great idea," but actually, it's not something that's important, not something that's going to add value to my life. And I don't have time for it.

[00:09:17.06] - Gordon
And these things change over time. Things that aren't important now could be important later in life. You might find your situation changes, and all of a sudden, that has become really important again. So that idea will still be in the back of your mind. And if you dry up with work and you find you've got nothing, well, maybe some of these old ideas to put out a service or a new product or whatever will come back to you and you can revisit them.

[00:09:44.07] - Taylor
Yeah, definitely. And it's one of those where if it's important enough, it will come back, but it frees up your head space and things like that, where you haven't got these lingering projects that you don't want to say no to because you don't want to leave them because you like the idea, but actually they were more bogging you down because they were just another thing in your to-do list when you look and you go, "Oh, I've got all of this to do." It's actually...

[00:10:11.25] - Gordon
Whereas you want to look at it and go, "Yes, I've got all this to do. I'm really looking forward to this." Now, that's where you want to be because that's when you're going to do your best work. Anything else you want to say on that?

[00:10:23.01] - Taylor
I don't think so.

[00:10:24.08] - Gordon
We'll put a link to the book that Taylor mentioned in the show notes. So if that's something that you want to look into further, then do seek out this book and have a read. My topic today is admin. So it's a really tedious and boring job, but it needs to be done, especially if you are a self-employed person. You've got lots of jobs that you take on as a self-employed person that you maybe don't realise you're taking on. Things like accounts, invoicing, getting back to phone calls, enquiries, what other admin is there? Just general day to day running of your business, paying bills and making sure you've invoiced everyone. That's a big one. All these things take time. And as a self-employed businessman, they're not the things I enjoy doing. I didn't get into doing magic and building websites so that I could do admin. That's not what I wanted to do, but it's something we have to do. And the other side of being self-employed is it's always going to be you that does it. Now, you can outsource these things or you can have someone else that does it, but that then adds extra expense.

[00:11:49.22] - Gordon
And you need to weigh up whether bringing someone in to do that is going to be cost-effective for you, or if you're going to end up working just so that you can pay this other person. And not have anything left at the end of the day for yourself. And the other point is with admin, is that most of the time, for me in particular, the admin is things that only I can do because I know what I've said to the customer, or I know what needs to be written in specific terms, or I know what agreement or deal we made. And to be able to pass that information over to someone else for them to do it, is going to take just as long as it would take for me to actually do the job in the first place. So I might as well do it. Now, because this admin needs doing, it's something that we don't necessarily factor in when we are looking at projects. So when we say to someone, "yeah, I'll be starting that on Friday" and you're on Wednesday. Well, maybe you wanted to start it on Friday, but you then look and you see, "I've got all this admin I need to do, and it's got to be done because there's a deadline coming up, or HMRC needs paying, or I've got to get my accounts to the accountant," or whatever it is.

[00:13:09.08] - Gordon
There's always jobs like that that take much longer than you think they're going to take. And you don't normally account for that when you give a timeline for people. And so I think my lesson here through experience is to instead of give people the idea that, yes, we're going to get started on this next week, I give myself a bit of leeway. And I'll say, "look, yeah, what we'll do is we'll start this on..." And then say a couple of weeks time, three weeks time, whatever is right. I'll add one or two weeks onto my start date because I know that if I'm finishing projects, they never finish on time. There's always little bits and tweaks and sometimes big major issues that happen when you put a site live, for example, that you then have to deal with. And you can't give your full attention to this project to finish it off and fix all the issues that have arisen, if in the back of your head, you're thinking, "I told that customer I'd be starting their job yesterday, and I haven't had time to get round to it yet." So they're waiting for you to come back to them with, "Yeah, we've started.

[00:14:25.29] - Gordon
It's all going ahead." And the people with the project before are waiting for you to say, "Yeah, I've fixed all the issues. You're live." And you're in the middle with this overlapped time period where two people need your attention and your time, and you just don't have that time. And nobody, I don't think, has ever complained if you say to someone, "I'm going to start your project in two weeks," and in fact, you start it in a week. I don't think anyone's ever complained that you've started it early. So there's an upside to it. Admin is a big part of running a business. And that's why bigger businesses have an admin person. That is their job. My dad, he was an accountant for a company. He was the accounting department for that company. His job was to make sure that all the finances coming in and all the finances going out were all accounted for. So it wasn't an accountancy firm. It was just the department in the company. And that's what he did. And that company was big enough to have an in-house accountant. As a self-employed person, I'm not big enough to do that.

[00:15:39.08] - Gordon
And I don't wish to be either. That's the other thing. I don't want to get too big, where I'm trying to manage a team of people and making sure I've got enough work coming in to be able to pay all these staff members. I mean, for me, at my time of life, I don't want to take on that responsibility. I don't want the responsibility of making sure that other people can put food on the table for their families. If I was your age, I might consider it. If I thought I was in the position to do that and steady work was coming in and I was doing really well and I was turning work away, maybe I would consider growing, but I don't want to do that now. I've paid for my house, I've got a nice life, I'm not struggling by living week to week or month to month. And "where's the money going to come from to pay that bill?" I'm not in that situation, so I don't need to push myself any further than I am. And I quite enjoy the lifestyle that I have. I like getting up in the morning and going, "right, what have I got today? Am I going to do a show? Am I going to work on a new trick? Am I going to be building a website for someone? Am I going to be doing some graphic design?" There's different things that I do every day, and every day is different. And I can choose to maybe take a day off or go away somewhere. As long as I make sure I get my deadlines set and I make sure I meet those deadlines and don't upset anyone, then all is good. How do you feel admin is dealt with as far as time managing for you?

[00:17:26.06] - Taylor
Yeah, I think... I don't enjoy doing it. I try and schedule everything that I need to do so I don't forget. I just work through it and try and make it so that it's one of the things I can just tick off and do it, set recurring tasks that remind me to do things. Otherwise, I just forget or I just avoid it. So I try and face it head-on and try and put things in place that make it easier to get it done or get started on it, whatever it may be.

[00:18:00.00] - Gordon
And it always takes longer than you think. So you think, "okay, I've got to bring my accounts up to date," and you think "that should take me, I don't know, an hour or two." And you find, you look at your watch and you've spent all day on it and you still haven't quite finished. So yeah, admin is something you need to factor into your business and make sure you put time aside for it. One of the worst things you can do is not invoice people. I know a couple of people I've met, our colleagues or friends who the invoicing part is just not something that they ever did. And they got behind on paying their suppliers. They ended up having to then argue the case with the customers because they said, "no, we paid this." And it's like, well, now you've got to go and check to see if payment was received. And that takes time. And then you got to go, "no, actually, it wasn't paid." And they'll say, "Well, yes, it was." And you go, "well, what date?" They then have to go looking. And then you've got to see. And it takes way, way longer than it ever should. So get those things done.

[00:19:11.01] - Gordon
As soon as a project is done or you've got to a date when you know you've got to invoice. Just do it. Get it done, get it out of the way, and make sure you have a system to chase it, because if people just ignore your invoices, what system is going to remind you that they've not been paid? This is something that I started doing reasonably recently, but quite a long time ago now. So in the history of my business, it was maybe three quarters of the time I've been going that I started doing that for my Drayson Design side, and I wish I'd done it a lot longer. I had records to show me what was paid and what wasn't paid, but what I wasn't doing is chasing payments that hadn't been made after a reasonable time. And I now have system in place that's all automated because we like automation, don't we?

[00:20:03.06] - Taylor
We do.

[00:20:04.04] - Gordon
So there you go. So that's pretty much all I want to say about admin. It's not a fun job. There are some people who enjoy the admin, but then maybe they don't enjoy the job. So it swings and roundabouts, really.

[00:20:16.20] - Gordon
In that case, make sure you leave time to actually do the job. But, yeah, that's my experience. And the only reason I brought it up today is because this week has been an admin week. It's the end of the summer holiday. Everyone's getting back to school. Everyone's going back to a normal life again. And so it's back to making sure I get some sort of schedule going in my life and make sure I get back to the routine of everything. That's it from me.

[00:20:49.01] - Taylor
And me as well.

[00:20:49.28] - Gordon
Thank you so much for joining us. As always, please like, share, and subscribe. We are on YouTube, and it would be great if we get more people watching our videos.

[00:20:59.10] - Taylor
You can also go to our website thisweekwith.co.uk to find all of our past episodes and anything we may have spoken about.

[00:21:06.18] - Gordon
And of course, you can listen to us as a podcast on all the major podcast platforms or your smart speaker. Just look for "This Week With Taylor and Gordon," and our latest episode will come up for you. We'll be back with you next Friday at 1pm. Until then, if you have any comments, please let us know. We'd love to hear from you. We'd love to find out what you think of these episodes and if there's been anything you've taken away from it. But we'll be back with you next week. Until then, my name is Gordon, and I'm from Drayson Design.

[00:21:38.11] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

[00:21:40.25] - Gordon
Goodbye.

[00:21:41.09] - Taylor
Bye.

transcript:
[00:00:00.00] - Gordon
Hello

[00:00:09.13] - Taylor
Hello.

[00:00:09.29] - Gordon
My name's Gordon from Drayson Design.

[00:00:11.26] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

[00:00:13.21] - Gordon
And welcome to "This Week With Taylor and Gordon," a weekly podcast and vidcast where we talk about things that have affected our businesses over the last seven days. And thank you so much for joining us. It's been a very busy couple of weeks. I've been away, which is the reason we haven't had, I think it's two episodes now, but we are back and lots to talk about and not a lot of time to do it in. So let's get straight into it. Do you want to go first or shall I?

[00:00:42.08] - Taylor
You can go first this week.

[00:00:43.25] - Gordon
So while I was away, I had the opportunity to have my box renovated. Now, what happens is that I've got a box that I perform children's magic, and it's got all of my bits in it, and I can't ever get it renovated or changed because I'm always using it. And so the only time I can do it is if I'm ill or if I'm going away and I don't need it, and I'm going on holiday and I can't necessarily work it for when I'm ill. So, I gave it to a friend of mine called Jezo, who is also an entertainer, a very good entertainer at that, and gave it to him with a mock-up of what I need it to look like, gave him the graphics I want to be on the front and left it with him while I went on holiday. And I picked it up this week. I went on Tuesday up to Cambridge, where he's based, to pick up my box, and it looks amazing. It's really good. I got to use it for the first time on Wednesday, which was the day after, and took photos of it in place, and it looked really good, didn't it?

[00:01:54.08] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:01:54.26] - Gordon
I mean, before it was black with hand-painted white on it, and that was my old branding. And I've got my new branding, and it required a complete strip down, a sand, a fill, a paint, a sand, a fill, a paint. Apparently, there's four coats of paint on it in total. And then it was all put back together again. And he's done a fantastic job, and I'm over the moon with it. He's really done well with it. But it gave me an opportunity to go to Cambridge this last Tuesday to pick it up from him. And I asked if he was performing because he's a children's and family entertainer, and he was. And I asked if I could go along with him to his show. And he said, yes. So I got to go to his show at a Haven site, which is primarily... Holiday parks are primarily his niche where he does all his work. And I got to see the... Oh, is there someone at the front door? You go do that. I'll deal with this. I got to see him perform in front of a real audience. I've seen him perform in a competition situation, but not in front of a real audience of punters.

[00:03:19.03] - Gordon
This was a really good way of seeing how what we do affects an audience. I was watching the audience a lot to see how they were reacting, to see what they liked, what they didn't like. And holiday park audiences are very tough because you've got to grab their attention because they start by chatting with each other. That's when you get introduced. And you've got the bar, in this case at the back. You've got a shop which is selling lighty-uppy things and all sorts of other bits and pieces. You've got a place that sells food, and you've got all your friends sitting around a big table chatting, and it takes an awful lot to grab their attention and, more importantly, hold their attention. He did a really, really good job at this. He went out into the audience right at the beginning and managed to involve them, and everyone was watching to see where he's going. You've also got all the children sitting on the dance floor. Again, you've got to make sure that you control that situation so they don't climb onto the stage and potentially get hurt and all sorts of things. Yeah, he's such a nice guy.

[00:04:39.00] - Gordon
You can tell that in his performance. You can tell that just by chatting with him. That's why I knew that my box project was going to be in great hands when I handed it over to him. Sure enough, when I picked it up, it was just great. This is possibly the last time I'm going to rebrand the box. He gave it back to me with the paint that he'd used so that if I need to do any touch-ups, I have the paint. I'm going to make a note of what it is. If I need to get it again, I can. He added brand new wheels. The wheels I had, this is a box that I have had since I was 15 years old. That's 37 years I've had it now. It got painted at the time and it got repainted, and now it's been repainted again. But it had the original metal wheels on which were at an angle, two halves, and the bottom half was the bit that touched the floor. I don't think you can even buy those anymore. But he's upgraded those wheels to two small rubber wheels on each corner, and the two wheels at the back now have locks, so I can lock it in place to stop it moving, which is great. I've never had that before.

[00:05:56.03] - Taylor
That's good.

[00:05:57.01] - Gordon
He's painted the whole of it, including the inside. So all of where I put my props is all painted as well. So that all looks beautiful. The paint not only looks good, but it's because it's got four paints, it's tough wearing and it protects the wood as well. I also have this fablon, which is a felty material with sticky on the back that I've got on the top, which I've always had, and I've replaced that as well. He put it on for me. He's also put the same stuff on the inside at the bottom as well. Now all the props, when they're stored, are sitting on felt as well, which obviously protects it even more. It all fits in the new bag that I had made, which I was concerned about because there was new wheels. Basically, he's done a really good job. If you're an entertainer watching this and you're looking to have an apparatus or a prop, either made or renovated, then I can't recommend Jezo highly enough. He did a fantastic job. That's me. Let's go straight through to you.

[00:07:07.11] - Taylor
I want to talk about padel this week.

[00:07:10.11] - Gordon
Paddle? On a-

[00:07:12.05] - Taylor
No, the sport, the new sport padel. Padel is one of the fastest-growing sports at the moment. It's a cross between squash and tennis, of which both of those sports I play. They've just added padel courts to my local club and I have been playing it. I've played about three or four games now and it's great fun. You get encased in a glass cage and you play it similar to tennis with a net and two players, but you can hit it off the back wall and the glass and the side like in squash. There are some other rules too, and things, but it got me thinking that we have certain skills that can be applied to more than one thing. So for example, my business, I have the skills to build a website, to design. And recently I've started expanding that to building little web apps for myself to improve my life, to make things easier. So I built a currency conversion, basically a little calculator. When I was putting them into my bookkeeping, every time I got paid in dollars, obviously there would be a currency conversion fee and also then a fee to pull it out of the platform, I think it was Wise.

[00:08:43.21] - Taylor
And I had to figure out what the currency conversion was inside of ZOHO to make sure that all of my basically numbers matched up. Because even if they were one or two decimal points different in terms of the currency conversion that ZOHO pulled in from their exchange rate, it would pull the numbers out slightly. So this week, I wanted to talk about UI design. So I have been working on a project for a friend of ours, and it is building a booking system. Now, the booking system already exists. However, we have basically hit some issues where his customers are struggling to use it and struggling to understand. The way the booking system works is the customer puts their venue address in for their party. They put the date that they want the party and then also the duration, whether it's like a one hour show or two hour show. And it then shows them the time slots available to them, based on his calendar. But what it does is it makes sure that the calendar shows the time slots calculated by the travel times. If the travel time was half an hour there, half an hour from, and then the show was one hour, you would need to make sure there's a two-hour window between the two events that he's already got in the calendar.

[00:02:10.16] - Taylor
So, the way it worked before is you just filled in the input fields and it then populated a select field like a drop-down. However, the people that were using it said they struggled because it wasn't easy to change or see a different day. Say they looked at a Saturday, they couldn't see, "Oh, is it actually easy, more free on a Sunday?" It was a bit finicky. So, what we've done is we've actually taken some ideas and inspiration from other calendar tools, and we've made our own version of that. [00:03:21.27] - Taylor

[00:04:00.10] - Gordon

So have you written a plug-in that he's adding on to an existing system that you could then use on other websites as well, for example.

[00:05:35.19] - Taylor

It's very good.

Well done. Anything else you want to say on that?

[00:07:00.08] - Taylor

[00:08:15.29] - Gordon
Something that was quite relevant to this came through my email last week, something that I think you would have got as well from a gentleman who runs The Admin Bar. His name is...

[00:08:33.09] - Taylor
Kyle.

[00:08:33.26] - Gordon
Thank you. Kyle Van Duzen. And he sends out a newsletter every week. And the one that I just received was really, really interesting. So he was listening to his customers, and sometimes they would come on the phone or they would come over email and they would say, "Oh, that's really expensive, isn't it?" And the natural reaction for someone who's self-employed, who wants to make that sale is, "yeah, I guess it is. I can do it for a little bit less than that if you like," or "I can give you a discount," or "I can take something off the project list and do it cheaper for you." It's basically saying, "okay, so if they're going to take 30% off, why didn't they give me that figure in the first place?

[00:09:41.14] - Gordon
Does this mean that every figure I get from now on is going to be over inflated and he expects it to be cut down? Therefore, should I just, every time he sends me a quote, haggle with him or her and tell them that's not what I want to pay, I want to pay less." And that word will get around. So Kyle's solution, which came from another source, was to say, "Yeah, that is very expensive," and to agree with the customer and leave it at that. They then have the choice and going, "Okay, well, maybe I can get it cheaper, but now I've got to start over and I've got to go to another supplier and I don't know anything about that supplier, and are they going to actually be able to deliver what I'm asking for. [00:10:55.07] - Gordon
And that I thought was really interesting. So in the magic world for me, when I give people a price on how much my magic performances are going to be, I don't discount at all, ever. I tell them how much it is. And something I learned a long, long time ago is once you've told them the price, shut up. Don't say anything further. Let them think about it. Let them be the next person to say something. And if they come back and say, "That's very expensive," or, "That's more than I thought," my reaction has always been, "Okay, well, I completely understand. My performances are... They have been created over many, many years and I've got a lot of experience, but that comes with a higher price tag. And if that's too much for you, I completely understand. And I leave it at that, ready to walk away. And the number of times that they go, "Do you know what? Let's just do it." As the response is much, much higher than you would think.

[00:12:10.17] - Gordon
But you do need to be willing to walk away. You have to expect that there will be some customers who will walk away and you will lose the sale. It's something you need to decide for yourself, really.

[00:12:52.18] - Taylor
It's interesting that you do it one way for one business and the other way, and you have been doing it the other way for another, where you're very, very firm on your prices for the magic, but not so much on the web design side. [00:13:41.26] - Gordon
I think it's a really good question. And I think the answer to that is, with the magic, I know how much I want to make, or how much I believe I'm worth based on the time it's going to take me to fulfil that job. So if I'm doing, let's say, a corporate dinner, I know that I'm going to be there for maybe two, two and a half, three hours, and I know what my time is worth for a corporate dinner, and I know exactly what's involved in that. I know all my expenses, all my costs. I know how long it's going to take me to get from home to the venue, to do the job, and get home again. I know exactly the length of time it's going to take, and I know how much I want to earn and what my value is. And therefore, my price is pretty firm. That's how much it's going to be. If you don't want it, then I know that they will go to other people and other people will charge similar amounts. And there are some people who want me because they know me, they like my style, they like my performance, they've seen me before, they know what they're getting, that sort of thing.

[00:14:54.06] - Gordon
So people will come to me because they want me, and no one else will do. And therefore I know that because of that, they're not going to go elsewhere because elsewhere is not going to be me. With a product like hosting a website or doing an update service, that, again, is something I know how long it's going to take. I know what my costs involved are. I know how much I need to charge for that. They, again, are not negotiable. If people come to me and they say, "I want to host my website, it's already done, I just want to host it with you," then I know how much that's going to cost. It's a set price. Building a website is very, very difficult because...

[00:16:12.11] - Taylor
Do you, I mean, do you track?

[00:16:13.26] - Gordon
I don't, actually no.

[00:16:15.26] - Taylor
That's probably part of it.

[00:16:16.24] - Gordon

Whereas with the web, the technology is changing all the time, and I might have to learn a new skill to be able to do a particular website. We've got one coming up that requires us to deal with subdomains. Now, that's not something I've ever had to do before, so that's something that both of us are going to have to learn about.
