[00:17:37.04] - Taylor
There's something else that Kyle does, which I think I might have spoken about before, which is paid discovery. What he does is that before he even quotes for a project, he'll do what's called a paid discovery, and that's where he will sit down with them for maybe two, three hours. He will basically discuss everything with the customer that they want. He will then go away, take all of the meeting notes, and probably spend maybe another two, two and a half hours on it, writing up a very, very detailed specification document with everything that they've discussed, and then from that, he will then quote for the website. Now, he doesn't include the project discovery inside of the total cost. So if they decide to go with him to build the website, then it's the paid discovery plus the website. If they don't, well, he hasn't lost any of the time that he spent mapping out the entire website, but that customer can then take that document that he's worked on and take it to another company. And the company that they end up going with is most likely going to be very very thankful because he's pretty much given the company the roadmap to "this is what the client wants." It's detailed enough that there's not going to be any surprises where they're like, "Oh, can we add on this page," it's like, "Well, that wasn't originally what..." [00:19:16.19] - Gordon
He's also being paid for his time to do that. So if they decide not to go with him, he's still being paid for his work.

[00:19:22.28] - Taylor

[00:20:24.27] - Gordon
That is for performance of magic, yeah.

[00:20:27.18] - Taylor

Let me ask you a quick question. Is that something you're now doing?

I think it's doing it the first time and either being rejected or having it accepted, that is the hard part, being up front and say-

It's mainly targeted toward web designers, but most of the stuff he talks about applies to pretty much any business apart from the specific ones, like the paid discovery that I know he's done a newsletter about. But you could still probably pull out information.

So this week, I want to talk about how you manage your work when you're self-employed and you work pretty much by yourself.

[00:02:08.02] - Gordon
Okay.

[00:02:08.29] - Taylor
Something that you have to do when you are self-employed and you have to create the tasks that need to be done. What this means is that for every single bit of work that you have to find, first of all, so you have to go out and find work, you then have to then figure out what work needs to be done; you then have to write down what that work looks like. You then have to actually do the work. You then have to check the work, and then you have to then approve and submit the work. Quite a lot of things you have to do. And I have always, for the most part, struggled with project managing and trying to keep track of projects and things like that, because what happens is I'll add in a task and do it then and there as I add the task in.

[00:03:02.04] - Gordon
Pardon me.

[00:03:02.28] - Taylor
What that means is you're doing a lot of context switching. So I was reading a book called "The Productivity Ninja," or "How to be a Productivity Ninja." I was also listening to a talk a couple of weeks ago. And what they said is that you have to have two sides to your business, essentially, and you have to wear two different hats. But these hats have to be completely independent of each other. There cannot be any overlap. You can't be wearing them at the same time. And so the idea behind it is that at one point you're a project manager. So you're the person that is doing basically all the speccing of tickets and making sure that you figure out what you need to do. And I also had, since I started doing some work for another company that is in a more corporate environment, they work in what's called sprints. And you have somebody that will create and manage all of the tasks that need to be done. They will take in the tasks requested by things like other people in the team, and then they will spec it out to exactly what is needed from that ticket, so what needs to be added or done, and what the success criteria looks like. And if it's a bigger task, they will break it down into smaller tasks. I found this a really enjoyable experience. I think if it's done properly, then it should be really really easy for a developer. And so, I took that and tried to implement it in my own business. So the idea is that, as I said, when you're the project manager, all you're doing is you're thinking about what needs to be done, all of the different tasks. If there's bigger tasks, then you break those down into smaller tasks. And you're basically writing a spec for yourself. So you're being very, very clear saying, "this is what needs to be done. This is what a completed ticket looks like." If there are any external things, so any resources or anything else that is relevant to that ticket, it's all should be contained inside of that. And then I then switch my hat, my invisible hat, and then I'm the doer. All, what I do when I'm the doer is, I look through the... Because I set up as a Kanban board. I look through, I pick one task, I do that, I move it to the completed column, I pick another task. And I don't think about anything to do with "what do I need to do next?" Because when you're doing that, you're having to context switch between trying to figure out at the same time of trying to do it. I found this method has started to work because I don't have to think heavily what I'm trying to do, in the same way.

[00:06:05.05] - Gordon
Well, you do have to think heavily because you're making sure you get what you do correct. But what you're not doing is thinking about something different. You're thinking about just that one task.

[00:06:13.19] - Taylor
Yeah. So it helps me to not context switch between doing six tasks at once because I open up one task and have that on the screen, so I can't do anything else. And I try and force my brain to not think about what else needs to be done. I will go through and finish the list of all the tasks. And then if I decided at a later date, "actually, I need to revisit this and check," then I'll go and inspect more tickets, review all of the tasks that are done. It's also really nice because I can add blockers. So, blockers are really nice because it means that although I know that I can't do those tasks yet, I can associate another task with that. So I can essentially say, "You can't do this task until this other task has been done." But I can still add it in there while I'm doing in the planning phase. So yeah, that's what I've been up to recently. I'm really enjoying it, and it's helped a lot for, like I said, the context switching, trying to do five, six different things at once, and also trying to figure out things on the fly and being a lot more meaningful in both my strategy and my planning, and then also being more productive in the doing because I don't have to try and maintain so many things.

[00:07:32.05] - Gordon
You mentioned a book which we'll put a link to in the show notes, but you recommend that book?

[00:07:38.28] - Taylor
Yeah, I really enjoyed it. There were lots of things from that book. This was just one of them, and when I also had the talk that I listened to that said things along the same line, that's when I clicked that, I was like, "Okay, I need to give us a look."

[00:07:54.29] - Gordon
Well, we'll come back to you, I think, in the future and see if you're still using that method or if you've refined it in any way, or decided not to do it at all. That would be a very interesting discussion. Before we move away from your topic and you, do you want to tell us how you got on with your 75 day challenge?

I'd go out for a walk, for example, at 11pm at night, which I don't recommend, but things just happen and life gets in the way, but I managed to do them. I think the trickiest things, or from what I thought would be tricky and what was actually the trickiest, it was probably quite interesting. So I thought probably cutting out fizzy drinks and energy drinks would be one of the hardest. There were lots of things that actually tried to force me to get fizzy drinks, especially when you get any takeaway or anything. It's either you get a fizzy drink or you get water. Eating the 2,500 calories was a lot because I always had to think, "what are my plans for my next meals?" Using prep kitchen helped a lot because it meant that I didn't have to think as much about what I was having for lunch, for example. I was normally having cooked meals in the evenings with the family and stuff. But yeah, it was always a matter of "what am I going to eat, when am I going to eat?" And then water as well was another one is trying to drink the water throughout the day. Otherwise, I end up chugging 2 litres almost in the evening, which isn't fun. They're probably the two hardest things I found. Probably the next bit after that was probably the exercise, especially when we were at family gatherings over Christmas and things like that, and it was very difficult to get them in because you don't want to seem rude, but at the same time, you need to go for those walks or whatever to get those two 45 minutes in, especially when one was outside.

[00:10:30.29] - Gordon
Yeah. So, just very quickly and briefly, what are you keeping and what are you not keeping from your challenge?

[00:10:38.18] - Taylor
I'm still figuring it out. I haven't really stuck to anything since I finished. I've just been enjoying being able to have fizzy drinks again and enjoying not having to be so strict. I still want to do my exercise. I still enjoy being active, just not to the level of feeling bad or guilty if I don't go.

[00:11:03.04] - Gordon
So maybe we'll come back next week and you'd have had another week to think about it and you can let us know what you are going to keep and what you are happy to let go.

Yeah.

[00:13:35.27] - Gordon
You're there in case anyone messes up and you can go, "Whoa, hang on, let's see, the audience aren't understanding this. Let me just explain." And carry on that way. That's always fun. Being with a whole group of people doing a show is very different to what I would do normally when I'm out performing. So, if I'm out doing a magic show, it's me. I'm the set putter upper. I put all the scenery up. I bring all the props in. I sort out my own costume. I don't wear makeup, but were I to be on somewhere where there's lights, then I possibly would.

[00:14:27.17] - Taylor
You have full control of everything.

[00:14:29.14] - Gordon

There's a lot of people involved, and it's really good to share this experience with other people. It makes it a lot more fun. And that's one of the reasons why I do pantomime, because I'm working with others and I'm collaborating with them and we're taking the script that's given, we're listening to the director as to what they want, and then we're making the show as good as we possibly can be, so that the audience get to enjoy it more. There's 180 seats per performance, and we've completely sold out on the Sunday afternoon.

[00:15:44.24] - Gordon
The last Saturday, I think we've got something like five tickets left for the afternoon and then something like 30 for the evening. We're doing really well. As we do the performances, people will talk to other people and we'll get people coming in to watch the other shows as we go through the week. The other reason I do it is because I'm honing my skills. Not only performance skills and acting and singing and dancing in this case, but also theatre skills. We've got other people in there. I didn't mention them before, but we got the lighting guy and we got the sound people. So I can learn from them. I can see what they're doing. One of the lighting people involved is involved with the National Theatre. So they know what they're doing. They've got all the software, they've got all the lights. They know how to light a set and a scene.

[00:17:00.00] - Gordon
And that's the thing that I'm learning. I'm looking, going, "Oh, that's very interesting. They're doing that, they're doing that." And it's all going in, and I'm learning it through osmosis, basically, just seeing it around me and absorbing the knowledge. And it's the sort of knowledge that you don't really come across easily, unless you seek it out or you're in an environment like this where you have professionals doing that sort of thing. And that's why I do it. So mainly for fun. It's my downtime. It's a hobby. It's something I do for fun. And secondarily, secondarily, is that a word?

[00:17:43.17] - Taylor
Secondary.

[00:17:43.29] - Gordon
Secondarily. Secondly... Let's go with that one. Sorry, Hayley, you're going to have to deal with that. Hayley is the one who transcribes all this. She'll have to figure all that out. [00:00:09.01] - Gordon
Hello.

[00:00:09.11] - Taylor
Hello.

[00:00:09.22] - Gordon
My name's Gordon from Drayson Design.

[00:00:11.15] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

[00:00:13.11] - Gordon
And welcome to "This Week With Taylor and Gordon," a weekly podcast and vidcast, where we talk about things that have affected our businesses over the last seven days. And welcome back.

[00:00:23.07] - Taylor
Welcome back.

[00:00:23.26] - Gordon
Thank you for joining us. Been a busy week again. I feel like I say that every week, but I do like to fill my weeks with things. So any news, first of all?

[00:00:36.02] - Taylor
Not from me.

[00:00:37.08] - Gordon
No, I don't think there's any from me either. So let's get straight into our topics. Right, do you want to go first?

[00:00:42.23] - Taylor
I'll go first this week.

[00:00:43.22] - Gordon
Go on then.

[00:00:44.11] - Taylor
My topic this week is about a 75 day challenge. So at the beginning of the week on Monday, well on Sunday I decided it, but I decided to start a 75 day challenge where I have a set of things that I need to do, and it's based on a well-known or an established challenge called the 75 Day Hard. And what the challenge is, is you have to drink a gallon of water. You have to do two 45 minute workouts, of one of which has to be outside. You need to stick to your diet, whatever you decide that to be. You're not allowed to drink alcohol. You need to read 10 pages of a non-fiction, and you need to take a progress picture every day. So I modified it slightly to work better for me with my Crohns and just in general, my goals. So mine is very similar. So two 45 minute workouts, 10 pages of a book, a photo, 2 litres of water, which is four and a half... A gallon is four and a half litres, so 2 litres, which is kind of the recommended. And my nutrition is minimum 2,500 calories eaten, 100 grams of protein, and cutting out fizzy drinks and energy drinks. So that is my 75 day challenge. So that will take me to the third of January. And the reason I started it was because I wanted to prove to myself that I could be disciplined and stick to something that I set myself out to do. For example, drinking water is not something I've actually really done. I didn't really like the taste of it, but it's good if I have electrolyte tablets, it's good for my stoma. And yeah, just trying to cut down on things like fizzy drinks, which aren't great. And also increase the food, increase protein, and stick to something at the gym going regularly.

[00:03:01.19] - Gordon
That's very good. And whose challenge is this?

[00:03:04.20] - Taylor
I can't remember his name. I think his name's Andy something, I want to say. So he started it, he called it the 75 Day Hard challenge. And there's also the 75 Day Soft, which is, again, a slightly simpler or less strict version. And I customised it to myself because cutting out alcohol would be very, very easy. I don't really drink alcohol anyway. So I thought, let me customise it to suit something that I would find challenging. So yeah, it's going to be interesting. There's a lot of things that I have to think about throughout the day to make sure that I'm hitting all of those targets. So making sure that I'm eating, making sure that I'm eating stuff that has protein in it, for example, making sure that I am scheduling workouts based on what I'm doing. There's no point just going about my day and not thinking about that, because then I'm going to get to seven o'clock, eight o'clock in the evening, go, "I haven't done any workouts." And a workout doesn't have to just be the gym. It could be a dog walk, it could be playing squash, play tennis, any type of physical activity where I'm getting out or doing something essentially. And that's the goal for it, really. And yeah, it's a lot about mental discipline, physical discipline, and just being able to... Have you ever done something like that?

[00:04:33.13] - Gordon
No, not at all. I'm not really a gym sort of person or an exercise sort of person. I do exercise when I'm doing my parties because that's a bit of a workout for me, especially carrying all the equipment in, setting it up, taking it all down, bringing it out, etc, etc. But yeah, that's probably the only exercise I do.

[00:04:53.06] - Taylor
This challenge isn't about keeping fit or trying to be better at being fit. It's more about being disciplined and having that mental resilience to, if you say you're going to do something, do it. There's been lots of times in the past year or so where I've gone to bed and I've thought, "I'll get up and go to the gym if I'm up," sort of thing. Whereas if you say, "I'm going to go to the gym in the morning," funnily enough, you actually get up. Whereas if you say "maybe," it doesn't really happen. But yeah, it's less about the fitness side of it. It's more about setting yourself a challenge that is actually going to challenge you and following it through and sticking to it.

[00:05:33.28] - Gordon
And what's the normal goal for this 75 day challenge? Is it to make sure you do keep disciplined, or is there like you're going to look better, feel better at the end of it?

[00:05:45.09] - Taylor
I think there's a lot of by-products from it. You're going to build up resilience. You're going to build up habits, like good habits and things like that. But most of it is building up the mental discipline to actually follow through with what you say. And the actual rules say that if you don't complete one of those five goals or challenges in a day, you go back to day one again. So the whole point is to complete the 75 days, which is what I'm going to do.

[00:06:20.23] - Gordon
So gamifying, looking after yourself, basically.

[00:06:24.09] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:06:24.25] - Gordon
Yeah, that's good. It's very good. Well done. We shall come back to this in January, shall we?

[00:06:31.17] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:06:32.05] - Gordon
And then you can tell us how far into your 75 days you've got, based on whether you had to restart or not.

[00:06:38.11] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:06:38.26] - Gordon
Very good. Anything else you want to say on that?

[00:06:41.22] - Taylor
I don't think so. I just think if you can set yourself a challenge, it doesn't have to be, I guess, as extreme as the challenge that I've gone for. But if you're able to set yourself challenges, it takes you outside of your comfort zone and you're always going to be improving and doing better.

[00:06:56.06] - Gordon
I agree. So my topic this week is use the things that you have. So this week I've had a couple of things that have happened. One is that I've got a customer of mine that I do filming for, and he's got a marketing company now that are going to be creating assets for social media and so forth to then get his name out and about to prospective customers; show them what he does. And I've done many films for this guy before, and whenever I've done them, we've always used them on a website. So I've always filmed them landscape and on my digital SLR or prior to that, it was on my tape camera. But because the marketing company want to do social media with it, they have requested that we do portrait video filming. Now, you can do portrait video filming on a DSLR. It's not ideal, though, because you're basically having to hold a camera that's quite heavy at an angle that's not very comfortable and therefore is going to not necessarily be stable. It then requires during the editing process to flip it so that it's portrait because that's not the native format of it, etc etc. So I thought, "Okay, for this challenge, what I'm going to do is I'm going to use my DJI Osmo Pocket 3, which is a little portable camera with a little screen that flips out so that you can have it either landscape or if you want, you can record portrait. But it does it at high quality, which is what I need. And that is what I'm going to use. Now, my only concern with this is I've never used it for a professional job before, so I needed to gen up on it and make sure I knew what I was doing and where the settings were so that I wasn't going to be sitting there while we were supposed to be filming going, "Hang on, just give me a second. I know the settings here somewhere." And make sure I know where everything is. And I'm also going to be using my DJI Mic 2s, which are a system which are wireless mics. We used them once before on this and I hadn't got the hang of them and it didn't come out great. And I think I know why now, because I wanted to make sure that I was all ready for it again. So it's coming up tomorrow. I'm filming tomorrow. I've been looking up and making sure I understand all the things I need to for being able to attach these mics to one to my customer who's going to be performing, and the other one is going to go on to the person he's performing to. And that way I can get clean audio from each of them without having to put a rifle mic or a gun mic onto my camera because it's just not big enough. The quality of the camera is good, but the audio is not so good because it's coming into it, whereas using the mics is going to give me much higher quality. And I've never done this before. I've never used them in that combination before. So I need to make sure that it's going to work. And by doing that, I'm going to make sure that I do some tests, first of all. And there were a couple of things while I was just looking through them that I didn't know they did, which is really good. One is that it's got a sync to video feature. So what happens is when you start recording on the camera, it will also record from the microphones. Now, I don't mean recording into the camera; because they're wireless the audio is coming straight into the camera and being recorded in the camera. But it's also backing up the audio by recording it on the mics themselves. So they have their own memory chips in them and they can record directly to the mics. So you've got not only a backup, but you've got a separate audio feed for each person, which you can then take afterwards and it gives you more options when you're editing. And I didn't know it did that. So that is really handy to know. And the other thing I didn't know it did is that you can actually plug in USB-C headphones to the camera and plug them into your ears so that you can then hear what's coming into the camera. So very easily, you can find out if there's any issues with the audio while you're recording, which is what I always do when I use my DSLR, but I've never used it with this camera because I didn't know it was possible. However, I didn't have USB-C headphones, so I'm using lightning headphones that came with my phone, in fact, came with my iPhone, but they've got a lightning connector on the end. And just by putting a little dongle in that I already had, which makes a lightning into USB-C, I've now got what I need to be able to hear. And it means that I can check the audio as it's recording. And if there's any problems, I can stop there and then and say, "Look, so sorry, we lost audio. Can we go again?" And we can do it again. And I'll know that the footage that I'm collecting is going to be fine. So that's the first thing that I wanted to mention. That's happening for my customer tomorrow. And then we're going to do another one in about a week's time as well. So it'll be good because I'll be able to learn from this experience and see what I need to change or add to the next time I do it to make it even better. Because obviously we're learning all the time, even if it's something we've done a lot. So that's the first thing. The second thing is I've got a website called facethepodcast.com, and it's a website for family and children's entertainers, and it's one that I started last year. It's a new podcast, and vidcast, where I talk to children's and family entertainers, and I haven't been recording any interviews recently. The last one I put up was back in February of this year, and that's not good enough because people really like them. And I've had lots comments about how they've enjoyed the episodes that I have up there, there's seven episodes. And if you go to that website, it looks very similar to This Week With. And that's because we took the whole infrastructure of This Week With and migrated it over and gave it a new facelift so that it met the criteria for what it is that I'm recording there. But I have restarted it again this week. I think what the problem is, is you get out of the habit of doing things, and this links in nicely with what you're talking about with your challenge. You get out of the habit and other things take its place, and the time that you have to do these recordings and to find people to do the recordings, and then the long process, which is actually the editing, all gets swallowed up with other things. Life gets in the way or work comes in. We've been working hard on lots of things; a website in particular has taken up quite a bit of time, but that's going to be launched soon, so that will be finished. And so I've started recording again, and I've already lined up another two dates where I'm going to be recording two other people. So I'm going to be having recordings coming in. And as soon as I've got the recordings, it's then down to me to edit them. But if I've got the recordings to edit, it will push me to then actually edit them and get them up and out so that I can then get on to the next ones. And they'll be up there as a record and an archive of these people and what they do and how they do it, which is what that podcast is all about. And I was neglecting it. I wasn't using it. I wasn't uploading to it. And so it fits in with my topic this week of using what you have. So if you've got equipment, if you've got software, if you've got a website that's waiting for content, then use it. Get on with it, or shut it down. That's the other alternative, isn't it? If you're not going to use it, then if it's a physical product, then sell it so that someone else can make use of it. And if it's a website, shut it down. But you obviously started these things or you bought these things because you had something in mind to use it for. So I would recommend, personally, get out there and use it, and you'll find out very quickly if it's the sort of thing that you want to continue doing or not. And if you don't, then don't waste time on it. Shut it down, sell it, get on to the next thing. Don't linger and go, "Yeah, one day I might get back to that," because it never happens. You'll end up with it sitting there for a year, two years, three years, And you'll go, "Oh yeah, I really should get back to that." And by that time, it's too late. So that's pretty much all I want to say. Is there anything you want to add to that?

[00:16:40.02] - Taylor
I think that if... Yeah, like you said, I think the best way to do it would be to schedule stuff and set yourself goals. So if you want to do X number of podcasts a year, schedule them in. Reach out to people and say, "look, I'd love to interview you. Are you around next year?" And schedule them in throughout the year next year, and then you've got them in there. And then obviously, it's just a matter of doing them. And then you've just got to edit them.

[00:17:08.23] - Gordon
Yeah. And by having somebody else having it in their diary, you feel like you need to do it. It's that compliance thing, not the compliance thing. It's when you know there's someone else involved and you don't want to let them down.

[00:17:23.13] - Taylor
Accountability.

[00:17:24.26] - Gordon
Accountability. That's the word. Thank you so much. Yeah, it's the accountability and making sure you actually do what you say you're going to do, but have someone else involved. So it's not just you that has to do it. That's it from me.

[00:17:38.05] - Taylor
And me as well.

[00:17:39.02] - Gordon
Thank you so much for joining us. As always, we can be found on YouTube. Please like, share and subscribe.

[00:17:45.26] - Taylor
You can also go to our website thisweekwith.co.uk to find all of our past episodes.

[00:17:50.21] - Gordon
And if you ring that bell on YouTube, if you are subscribing, then it'll tell you when our next episode is out. So you can be alerted that way. If you would prefer to listen to these, then we are on all the major podcast platforms. You can find us there. If you find a platform that doesn't have us, then let us know and we'll do our best to get on there because we want to make sure we're available to as many people as possible. We'll be back with you next Friday at 1pm. Until then, my name is Gordon, and I'm from Drayson Design.

[00:18:25.14] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

[00:18:28.01] - Gordon
Goodbye.

[00:18:28.12] - Taylor
Bye.

Hello.

Hello.

[00:00:10.04] - Gordon
My name's Gordon from Drayson Design.

And I'm Taylor from the Creative Tinker.

And welcome to "This Week With Taylor and Gordon," a weekly podcast and vidcast where we talk about things that have affected our businesses over the last seven days. And welcome back if you've been with us before.

[00:00:24.18] - Taylor
Welcome back.

[00:00:25.22] - Gordon
It's been a busy week for me. I've had lots of shows, lots of things going on. I've had my drama teaching classes which are going well. And as it happens, the class went really well, so I was really pleased. [00:01:40.03] - Gordon
Very good.

[00:01:41.14] - Taylor

[00:01:45.22] - Gordon
Lovely. Okay, so let's get straight into our topics for the week. Would you like to go first?

[00:01:52.06] - Taylor
You can go first this week.

[00:01:53.26] - Gordon
Okay, mine's going to be quite simple today. I was out collecting a package that was delivered, or attempted to be delivered, yesterday and no one was here. And so UPS, in their wisdom, decided to drop it off at a dry cleaners and then tell me that's where they were going to put it. Now, that's all well and good, but the dry cleaners in question is in the middle of a town. Parking is impossible, and it took me about an hour, about an hour to go and get it. And I was really upset because it was just too much time out of my day just to do something like that. And that was only one of the packages I was expecting. I didn't realise there were two packages. And the other one arrived when I got home. It's like within 10 minutes, the package arrived. But they've changed the way they do things, but I'm not sure they've checked with their customers to see if they like it. So I said to the man when he arrived, I said to the UPS man, UPS. "I don't like your new system of dropping it off." He said, "Oh, where would be easier?" I said, "Well, just put it in a safe place like everyone else does when they deliver." He said, "Oh, okay." We've got a safe place that you can put packages if nobody's in. And UPS didn't want to do that originally, but I don't know if he took it on board. He said, "Okay," and walked off. But they've tried something new. While I was getting my package, I happened to go in and get myself a packet of crisps and a drink, and I came across a can of Tango, which is mango-flavoured, which I'd never seen before. It's sugar-free, which I don't normally like, but I do like mango, so I thought I would give it a go. And it's not bad. It's okay. Tango have tried something new, and they are seeing how it works in the marketplace. It might be that it's a limited edition. It might be that they're just going to see how it sells, find out if people like it or not, and then decide whether they're going to make it a continual product going onwards. But my point is that whatever it is you're doing at the moment, you may be able to offer variations or alternatives to it, and you might find that your customers like it and love it, want to do it, want to use it. You might find that they don't like it at all. Another example for you: we order food for our dog that comes in little packs, and we put them in the freezer and then every three days or so we get one out, we cut it into sixths and he has one sixth for breakfast and one sixth for dinner. And that's been working really well for us, for quite a long time now. And they've gone and made a change. So the next food that we order from them is going to be automatically cut into four pieces. So it's going to be in quarters, which is no use to us. We don't want quarters, we want sixths. So I emailed them back and said, "Great that you're trying something new. This won't work for us, though. Can we make sure we just get the normal food without any cuts in it or impressions in it?" And they came and they said, "No, it's for everyone now. All of our food is being done like this." It's like ahh, so they got the feedback from me that it's not great because it's going to make our life just that tiny bit more difficult. I mean, it's not a lot more difficult going from quarters to six, but when you have just a normal slab of meat, if you like, cutting it into six is nice and easy. If it's already cut into four, that's not so good. So they're trying something new, and I've told them that I don't think it's going to work for us and it depends if everyone else says the same. Our dog is going mad. Do you want to have a quick look? See if there's someone there. There might be someone at the door. So, yeah, what I am trying to say is that you should try new things, research them, and then just get feedback and find out if it's the sort of thing that your customers want and like, or if they don't like it and they don't want it, in which case you can scrap it and have a look and see if there's anything else new that you can try. So that is it, really. I'm sure there's going to be some people who can take something away from that. I think I should take something away from that and continually update and improve my product range and see if there's anything that I can do that my customers like better than what I'm doing at the moment. That's it. What would you like to talk about?

[00:07:04.21] - Taylor
So mine actually follows on quite nicely from yours. Mine is about iterating your processes and also iterating your products. So I have a child theme/starter site that I've built and I've probably put 40 plus hours maybe into it. And it's not something I've put 40 hours into straight away. I probably put a good couple of weeks in and spent a majority of my time working on that. However, what happens is as I'm building out new sites, I come across the need for a new functionality or I go, "that would be quite useful. And I've done this on three sites now, maybe I should add this into the core of my child theme." So what I've been doing is I've been iterating as I go. So as I'm building out sites and I've come across something that I've done more than once or I've gone, "actually, that might be quite useful. I could make this a standardised thing that I can reuse in other projects." I will pretty much just load up my starter site then and there and integrate it. I have a running change log of all of the changes that I've made and I've added version numbers so I can keep track of what was added and what's got, what's new, what's changed, what's been fixed and things like that.

[00:08:24.23] - Gordon
And that's important. If you go back to a site that you've done in the past and you need to add something, you can then look at the starter site version that you've got and see on your change log what's been added and if you need to update the starter site, for example.

[00:08:39.13] - Taylor
Yeah, exactly. A lot of the starter sites, I can't just update because they have a lot of custom code that are written for that site, but it at least gives me a ballpark of, "okay, this is the kind of functionality that I have. This is what I'm going to be missing because the change log has got later things. But I've been doing this in a lot of other places." I've been iterating on my processes for creating and managing my projects. I spoke about this a while ago where I created stages, and then I've pre-configured a lot of tasks that need doing so that there's a more standardised process, and so I don't forget things. It's very easy to forget things that need doing. If you've got them laid out and already set up as a boiler plate, it helps me really make sure that all of the steps are followed, all processes are completed. And there's been times when I've gone, "Oh, what do I need to do?" Because it's all written down, I just need to go through. Launching a website I used to hate. It used to take me ages because there's so many little things. But when I just broke it down and said, "this is what a launched website will look like," it takes maybe half an hour now. And that's because I've refined my process, looked at ways I can improve it, but also iterated upon it. If I find that something I'm doing is taking too long or there's a better way to do it, I've updated the process. And so it's just looking at ways you can keep iterating on your processes and your products, like you were saying, is adding new things in. If you add a new service or you add a new feature to one of the products, if you, for example, have a website care plan, for example, and you're adding something new in, see if your clients like it. And yeah, it's good to get feedback. And I don't think we ask enough about getting feedback. I manage a couple of different products and I get feedback regularly for those rather than my agency side. And I'm always trying to improve and try to make it better for the user, really.

[00:10:49.22] - Gordon
Yeah, I think it's good. Otherwise, you're just going to stay still and you're going to get stagnant and you're not going to be relevant anymore. We have to move and improve otherwise, we end up going backwards, really. So yeah, that's really good. Well done. Anything that you have seen recently that has come from these improvements that you've been making? Anything you can measure by? Because the reason for doing it is so that you get more customers, you can charge more, or it takes less time, or something else. So is there anything that you use to measure whether something has been worthwhile doing?

[00:11:26.22] - Taylor
No, but it's something I might look at doing in seeing if I can track how long projects are taking. I think that's probably the biggest one is tracking how long projects take and also how long each stage takes. I think is a very very good marker because it allows you to see where you're spending the most time and whether or not the reason you're spending the most time is because you're putting the effort into that, because of unforeseen things, or you're just not estimating properly of how long you think a project will take. And so that can help gauge, I guess, how long a project will take and also when you have availability next. If you can't measure-

[00:12:11.02] - Gordon
They have a knock-on effect, don't they?

[00:12:12.24] - Taylor

It's very much can be a he/she said argument if it's all on the phone. And the other thing is making sure you know what the next steps are. I find that sometimes I can forget. I come off a call and go, "oh, what was that thing I wanted to do?" And you can't go back to the client and say, "what was that we said?" Because it just looks unprofessional. So, I've had this multiple times where I've had a conversation with someone, a client, and then because of the workload or whenever something is scheduled for, it's being done in a month's time, for example. But sometimes they're very very brief and they mean something to you in the moment. However, coming back to it in a month's time, six months, a year, six years time, you may not know what the reference was meaning. [00:07:36.06] - Taylor
Good.

Very good. That leads quite nicely onto my topic. Sticking with AI, we spoke about it last week. There's been a new development, as there always is every week, and this is with Open AI's ChatGPT. They've now come out with, for some people, you've got a voice chat that that's being rolled out so you can talk to people on your phone or on your device, and it will talk back to you like a person. And it has all of the ChatGPT features available to it. So you can actually just sit there and chat to it, which is pretty amazing the first time you try it. It's like talking to a real person. It's so good. So that's really good. And just maybe gives us a glimpse into the future as to where we're going to be going with this sort of thing, because Siri is going to be coming up with this sort of chat to it, artificial intelligence type thing as well. So it's becoming more like Star Trek every day, where they used to just say "computer" and then ask it something. It's going to be just like that. But OpenAI have also come out with a new feature for those who code or who write documents, whether that be a blog post or an article or whatever. And it's called, I think it's called Canvas. So you can effectively, and this is really clever, up to now, if you had, for example, ChatGPT, write you some code from your prompt, you would then, if it didn't work, you would give it feedback and you would tell it what was wrong or what the error was. And it would then rewrite the whole of that code and give you a new version of that code, which you then test. And if that works all good, if not errors, it comes back and it will rewrite it again. But the Canvas is really good because you can have it just rewrite parts of the document. So let's look at it in a blog post situation. If you've asked it to write you a blog post, you've given it as much detail as you can. It's written the blog post and you think, "Yeah, I don't like the title." You can just select the title and you can say, rewrite or change this so that it's more dynamic or more eye catching or whatever you want, really. It will just change the bits that you want at that time. And it's really good. Have you played with it at all?

[00:10:47.22] - Taylor
I haven't.

[00:10:48.14] - Gordon
Okay, it's really good. It's available on the web version, and I believe it's being rolled out to the app versions as well. I don't think so.

Well, there we go. A nice, sharp, short episode for you. As always, we can be found on YouTube. Please like, share, and subscribe.

And I should say our YouTube channel is "This Week With Taylor and Gordon." I think if you do a search for that, you'll find us. There are other This Week Withs, but there's only one "With Taylor and Gordon." We can also be found on all your favourite podcast platforms, so you can listen to us in the car, on your run, while you're exercising, however you like. Thank you for joining us. And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

Goodbye.

Bye.

That we should move all the slideshows into their own space; take them off my main website. And so we're using what's called a subdomain. Now, subdomains are very cool because, for example, my main domain is disbelieving.com, and then a subdomain is something.disbelieving.com, and the something can be anything you like. You can have as many subdomains as you like. So if you look at it in the way that Google do it, they have google.com, they've got images.google.com, they've got docs.google.com, they've got sheets.google.com. They're using an awful lot of different subdomains, and there's probably hundreds that we don't even know about that are just used internally. And so that's what we decided to do. Taylor came out with the idea of creating a layout and then bringing all the information that we need in dynamically. So basically, we're creating a post, we're putting all the information into that post, and then it will create the page for me. Which means that if I want to change the design or if I want to add something in the future, I can change the design on one page, the template, and all of the pages that I've ever done will automatically then be updated; which makes life a lot easier. I also added a picture, a photo, one of the photos from the photos that were taken, and added that on the page because I thought that was a nice little addition. There's two things we had to take into account here, though. First thing is that if people went to the old address, because that's where I told them to go, they need to then be redirected automatically to the new address. So we sorted that out. That was all done. The second thing is making sure that if a customer forgets the URL or they lose the email and they don't know how to see their videos anymore, an easy way for me to do it that's secure. So it doesn't allow people to just basically guess at a URL and hope that they'll find someone's slideshow because that's not secure at all. So the solution we came up with was to have on the homepage of this slideshow section is to have people being able to put in their email address. And I've got an email address that's attached to every different post. And sometimes people have more than one post because maybe I've gone back and done two or three parties for them. And so their email address will be in several posts. And then once you put that email address in, if it's an email that's recognized, it will then send an email to that person with the link or links to their slideshow or slideshows, and then they can click on those and go and have a look. And the other advantage to this is I can offer the customer the option of giving me other email addresses for other members of family, so that they can go and do the same thing. And that is a really nice way of doing it. For example, I have a joint birthday party. Well, I can take the email address of the second family or the third family, and I can send that to them as well. So it means that they get to see the slideshow and they can go in and do it as the person who booked me has always been able to do or will always be able to do. So that makes life really really good. And it just streamlines the process again. If anyone rings me up and says, "we had a slideshow with you, but I can't remember the address," I'll just say, "go to the address that we've come up with, the subdomain, and type in your email address, it'll email you." Or if I'm feeling like it's easier, I'll just go in and do it myself, type in their email address. It will send them an email and it looks like it's come from me and it looks like I'm the one that spent time finding the links and sending it to them, which again, is a really good customer service thing. Have I missed any benefits out?

The only other thing was the title generation.

Oh, yeah. That was a real logical nightmare, wasn't it?

[00:14:23.270] - Taylor
Yeah. So we had up to three children that you can add. And the way that the titles were formatted were, it was, for example, Taylor's 10th birthday party, for example. Now, if you have two people, it would be Taylor and Gordon's birthday party with the and as in the text rather than the ampersand.

[00:14:48.010] - Gordon
And the apostophe s only goes on the last name, not the first name as well. Otherwise, Taylor's and Gordon's 10th birthday party is wrong grammatically.

[00:14:57.620] - Taylor
Yeah. And then if you have three. It would be Taylor comma Gordon comma Bill, or and Bill's birthday party. Again, with the apostrophe s on the last one.

[00:15:08.530] - Gordon
Yeah.

[00:15:09.630] - Taylor
That is all good. However, if you have two children that have a birthday, but they are different ages, you'll then have Taylor's 5th and Gordon's 10th birthday party. And so both children need the apostrophe s, and you need to use an and to join them together.

[00:15:29.450] - Gordon
And you need to make sure you've got the birthday year and what do you call the bit after it?

[00:15:36.830] - Taylor
Ordinal suffix.

[00:15:38.190] - Gordon
An ordinal suffix. So three R-D, four T-H, 1 S-T, they're all different.

[00:15:47.270] - Taylor
Yeah, the endings of the number or the age. And then obviously, if you've got three and you've got two that are one age and one that's another, it would be Taylor and Gordon's fifth and John's second...

[00:16:00.910] - Gordon
Birthday party.

[00:16:02.460] - Taylor
Yeah. And then it would if we had more than three, if you had three, one age and one another, it would be name comma name and name, age. And then and, name, age. It gets a bit confusing, but we basically built it so that no matter what format or format we have it, it will build the title to be correct. And that is used as a slug. That's used for the title of the page. When we send them links, that's the name so they can see. And yeah, it just makes it really easy. And then it doesn't mean, you don't have to build or write out and figure out what the title needs to be.

[00:16:46.880] - Gordon
Yes. We've set it up so that I just fill in a form, basically. I just fill in. It asks for the first name, last name, age. Is there another child? Yes. Put the first name, last name, age in. Third child, first name, last name, age. The date, the link to the video, the link to the photos, the email address of the people who are allowed to get the email sent to them, and that's pretty much it.

[00:17:15.360] - Taylor
Yeah, it's quite interesting, mainly because if you update the child's name or the age or anything like that, it will automatically update the title and the slug, etc. We found that... We were going to do a dynamic redirect from your old site or your main site to the subdomain. And that would have worked perfectly fine if you had used the exact same formatting in every single-

[00:17:41.320] - Gordon
Which is one of the reasons we changed it.

[00:17:43.390] - Taylor
So for example, and some of them you had an apostrophe s on some of them, and in others you didn't.

[00:17:50.900] - Gordon
And that was because it wasn't something I was doing all the time. It was whenever there was a slideshow that was being done. So trying to remember the format, I didn't have a process for it, which I now do. And I can't remember... If I create a new post, does it automatically email the customer to tell them it's been set up? I can't remember.

[00:18:14.230] - Taylor
No, it doesn't.

[00:18:15.110] - Gordon
No. Okay, so that's good. It's a manual process, which is fine because that's how I want it, because every time I go in and make changes, I don't want it to then email the customer to say, "your slideshow's up. Here's the information," because they'll already have that.

[00:18:29.340] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:18:29.570] - Gordon
But it's a much better system now and makes my life a lot easier, makes the customer's life a lot easier, which is the important thing. That's the main point, really.

[00:18:38.760] - Taylor
Definitely.

[00:18:40.060] - Gordon
That's all I want to say about that. Do you have anything else you wish to add?

[00:18:44.380] - Taylor
I don't think so. It's a nice solution because it's scalable and it also takes it off the main site, which when you get to, how many do you have? 100 plus or whatever, you get to a lot of pages and then it becomes hard to manage it in the back end and you're ending up with lots of stuff that isn't really needed because it's not the primary function of the site.

[00:19:06.820] - Gordon
Yeah.

[00:19:07.030] - Taylor
So if you can, you should always try and move stuff to a subdomain.

[00:19:10.360] - Gordon
And that doesn't actually make a big effect on people visiting the site, but it makes the database a lot bigger and the search requests are going to take a little bit less time... Sorry, it's going to take a little bit longer because you've got so many more records to go through. So anything you can do to optimise your site will, in the end, make it better for everyone.

[00:19:37.630] - Taylor
Yeah, exactly.

[00:19:39.450] - Gordon
That's it from me.

[00:19:40.840] - Taylor
And that's it from me as well.

[00:19:42.230] - Gordon
Thank you for joining us. As always, you can like, share and subscribe. We're on Facebook and on YouTube.

[00:19:49.650] - Taylor
You can also go to our website thisweekwith.co.uk to find all of our past episodes.

Hopefully, we'll be back next week, assuming that everything goes to plan. Until then, 1pm next Friday, we'll see you for the next episode. My name is Gordon and I'm from Drayson Design.

[00:20:06.070] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

Goodbye.

[00:01:28.480] - Gordon
Okay, what are you going to talk about?

[00:01:29.620] - Taylor
So I came across... Well, I got sent a newsletter and it was about how you deliver design mock-ups to clients. Now, the way I normally do it is I just send them a link to a mark-up tool where they can click over the image and leave feedback. There was a couple of different ideas and solutions that were in the newsletter article. One of them was creating a physical version of the design, so you actually build the website and then give it to them so they can play around with it. That allows you to give them a more interactive solution. And the other one, or the other two were recording a video and explaining yourself going through the design, telling your client why you've done, made certain design choices; your ideas behind it in terms of what their end goal is. So you've designed this this way because this is how people tend to use a computer or use a website. And what it does is it negates the client from making purely emotional decisions and suggestions. So a big one we normally get is, "Can you make the logo bigger?" Other ones are, "Can you change the colour? Can you make stuff bigger? Can you move this a couple pixels to the left," or whatever? And these aren't really helpful feedback. These are purely, "this is what I feel my website needs to look like," when in actual fact, they're not taking into account their target audience, they're not taking into account their end goal. So if your end goal is for someone to contact you, you don't want to have them going to your social media, for example, as being one of the primary call to actions because that just goes against what your end goal is. And so it's all these things that the clients don't really think about and they just make suggestions and ideas based on how they feel when they look at the website. And so by giving them the video, it allows them to see why you've done something, which is obviously always important. And if they do share the design with people in their team, their company, they can obviously also share that design, that video, sorry, with the team as well. And so although-.

[00:04:06.110] - Gordon
Pardon me.

[00:04:11.020] - Taylor
Although people like to have design by committee where everyone likes to have their ideas and stuff, you can again try and minimise that by basically saying, "this is the reasons why we've done what we have." And then as long as you are making them aware of what their target audience is and what their end goal is when you're walking through it, they will also keep that in mind. And you need to be specific about the feedback that you want as well. So you may want to get their input on certain elements, but not the whole design. So it's also being specific about the type of feedback that you want rather than just 'make it bigger. Can you change the colour?' Things like that.

[00:04:53.280] - Gordon
That's very good. Is that something that you've now done or is that something that you are going to do?

[00:04:58.770] - Taylor
Next time that I send a design for review, I will make sure that I include a short video to go along with it to help get across my ideas.

[00:05:09.010] - Gordon
That's very good. I really like that idea. It's going to save a lot of potential issues with design discussions, which you can have between customers and yourself. And trying to get them to understand you're the expert as far as the design side of it comes, and they are looking to you to give them what they want. And sometimes they can get in the way of that, can't they?

[00:05:41.750] - Taylor
Yeah. So, I had a business coach and I did my three... I can't think what the word is, but three things that I go by in life, essentially. And you get this big-

[00:05:56.320] - Gordon
Key values.

[00:05:56.840] - Taylor
Yeah, key values. And one of the things that I found was with one of my clients was that I would present them with a design and things like that, and they would come back and say, "I don't like this, this, this and this." And to me, that hurt because one of my key values was already, or my geniuses, sorry, was that I'd already done all of the looking at all of the different ideas and finding the best possible solution. So when I had presented that to the client and sent them the link to look at, they came back and said, "Oh, I don't like that. I don't like this." And it's like, "Well, I've already done all of this work of what the best solution is, and this is what I've given to you. And when you go against that, it hurts inside a bit," because it's like, that's why I reacted in certain ways to that. It's nothing that the client had done, it's just the way that I go about my business, I go about my day to day life. And so again, this is a way to negate that from happening by explaining the reasons behind my decisions essentially.

[00:07:07.350] - Gordon
That's very good. Anything else you want to add?

[00:07:09.700] - Taylor
I don't think so. We can leave a link to the article that I was sent.

[00:07:15.130] - Gordon
Yeah, ok. So there'll be a link in the show notes that will be on the website and in the YouTube and Facebook description. Have a look at that. It will take a short while for that to happen, as always, because we have to do it manually. We can only do that once we've finished the recording of it. So that gets done afterwards. Have a look there for the link and you can have a read of the article and see if there's anything in there that will be of interest to you.

[00:07:41.920] - Taylor
Yeah.

[00:07:42.230] - Gordon
Thank you for that. That was really interesting. I quite like the idea. I'd like to talk to you about accounts. My week, pretty much, has been taken up by doing my accounts. Now, accounts is not something that we get into business to do. It's not one of the things that we go, "Yes, I get to do my own accounts now." And that's why I've passed my accounts over to an expert. I've given it to an accountant. But I still have to prepare them and present them. And the more work you do, the less money you have to pay to get your accounts done, basically. So if you can get yourself into some sort of system that works well with your accountant so that you can just very easily at the end of the particular term, export everything, send it over to them, and it's in a format that they can actually use, then you're going to save yourself time and money with somebody having to manually enter those details into their system again. So that's the first thing. Second thing is, by keeping your accounts up to date, you will always be able to see where your businesses are. So, I know a lot of people will leave things for most of the year. For self-employed people, we have to submit our accounts by the 31st of January. Now, I'm well ahead of that. And the reason for that is because I want to get them to my accountant to find out what my tax bill in January is going to be, which will then allow me to prepare and save and make sure I've got the money available for the tax bill. Because the last thing you want is to get to the 31st of January, you've just submitted your accounts, you get given your tax bill, and all of a sudden you go, "Well, I have no idea where that money's coming from." So by doing it ahead of time, you can negate all that. Now, last year, I decided I was going to do it before the July 31st payment date, which is for self-employed people, we pay every six months. The July one is 'payment on account.' You pay an amount based on your previous year's turnover. You pay, I think it's 50% of that again going towards next year's. And if you get your accounts in ahead of that date, you can actually reduce your 'payment on account,' they call it, which is basically you're actually paying for real figures, not estimated figures. Now, I did that last year and it caused a bit of confusion because I got to a point when I wasn't entirely sure what I should be paying. I had to talk to HMRC and say, "I'm bringing my payment on account down because these are my actual figures." I thought, "Do you know what? I quite like the idea of getting it in early, but I don't want to get it in before July 31st," because if you've had a really good year, you're paying a lot more on account for the next year. And if your next year is not so good, well, by the time you get to January, you're going to be paying very, very little. So if you haven't had a great year, that's a really good thing to do. So that's what I'm doing this year, and that's why we are after July now. In fact, we're in September now. Welcome to September, everybody. Back to school, back to a little bit of normality in some respects. The accounts will be sent to my accountant so that they can deal with it. It will take them probably two, three weeks or so. So by the end of September, I suspect my accounts will be in, which gives me October, November, December, January, four months, which is a third of a year, to actually get the money available and know what I need to pay. And that's a really big thing. I had in my accounts that I'm preparing, I had a purchase of a car. I know that that is going to bring my tax bill right the way down, possibly to nothing. In fact, the tax office might owe me money because of it, but I won't know that until the accountant has dealt with everything. I'm not too worried about my next tax bill because I know it's not going to be very high. I use a programme called Quicken, and there's lots of different applications you can use. There's Quickbooks. What do you use?

[00:12:23.210] - Taylor
Zoho Books.

[00:12:24.130] - Gordon
Zoho Books. There's lots of applications you can use to keep your accounts. But if you make sure that when you have payments that come in and you have payments that go out, that you keep track of them in some software, you will always have an idea of where your money is, your level, how much you have in the bank, how much you've got coming out, because it will have pending transactions for monthly and subscriptions and that sort of thing that come out. And you'll be able to make business decisions much easier, based on whether you can afford something or not, looking forward. You can see into the next two, three months, see what amounts are coming out and see if... Sometimes amounts coming in as well. You can make decisions as to whether a new bit of equipment or an upgrade is going to be viable or worthwhile or affordable, which is really important when you're running a business, especially a small business.

[00:13:26.330] - Taylor
Definitely.

[00:13:27.610] - Gordon
Do you find that you make decisions based on your bank account or your accounts?

[00:13:34.730] - Taylor
Mostly my bank. I just see how much is in there, but I do have a rough idea of how much I spend each month and how much I bring in. So I do a rough estimation.

[00:13:46.290] - Gordon
Yeah. And we're all in business to make sure that we can buy what we want and need, and support our families. So it's really important, the bottom line. And so by making sure you keep track of all this, you're going to make sure that you keep on top of everything, basically. So that is everything I want to say. The dog is barking. Is there anything you want to add?

[00:14:10.250] - Taylor
I don't think so. Just keeping on top of all your accounts and things like that not only keeps everything in order, but also gives you a lot of peace of mind. I have been in the past at points where I'm like, I don't know where my next payments are coming in because I've been ill and things like that. So it's not so much that I wasn't earning money, it's just I wasn't doing the work to get the money. So I had jobs and stuff that I had needed to be completed, I just wasn't in a good enough health state to be able to do it. And so I had my reserves essentially going down. And although it was hard to see that happening, I also kind of knew how much I was spending, so I could forecast how long is this going to last me essentially? And what do I need to do? What things do I need to put in place to make sure that doesn't happen again? So for me, it's very much building up a reserve of cash that I can put to a side and basically say, "this is for, should I ever get ill again." And also getting insurance can also be good for that. So I've got health insurance for exactly that thing. If something happens to me, I can get... I can claim money, essentially, to keep me from going under and things like that. And also if you are investing your money and things like that, you're going to be on top of your money if you're investing and things like that. And that, again, adds clarity to being able to decide whether you can afford to buy something and just what you have in assets.

[00:15:52.890] - Gordon
Well, you can also see if there's any problems with the business as well by watching the financials, because you can see if you are spending money on something that's not actually working well for your company, you can just stop it. You can stop the subscription, you can change the direction that you're heading in. You can do whatever you need to do to make sure that you don't spiral out of control, basically, because no one wants to be bankrupt. And the only way you'll know that is to be on top of everything. So the accounts are really important. It's not something I think we've spoken about much on here, but it's a really important thing for a business, any business, any size. Even big businesses need to keep track of their income and expenditure. And in fact, more so for them, because one big expenditure for them could be millions of pounds, which could put them bankrupt if it doesn't work for them. So any size business needs to make sure they know where they are as far as financials go. That's all I really want to say.

[00:16:58.850] - Taylor
Yeah, same for me.

[00:16:59.720] - Gordon
Thank you so much for watching. As always, you can find us on Facebook and on YouTube. Please like, share, and subscribe.

[00:17:08.710] - Taylor
You can also go to our website thisweekwith.co.uk to find all of our past episodes and anything we may have spoken about.

[00:17:15.380] - Gordon
And if you want to get in contact with us, please leave a comment or email us. We've got emails on our website. We'd love to hear your thoughts on anything that we've spoken about. Until next week, Friday at 1pm, we'll see you then. My name is Gordon, and I'm from Drayson Design.

[00:17:33.050] - Taylor
And I'm Taylor from The Creative Tinker.

[00:17:35.480] - Gordon
Goodbye.

Bye.
